name: A/B Testing
one_liner: When opinions clash, change one thing and let real behaviour decide.
teaser:
A/B Testing means showing two versions to similar groups and letting real behaviour pick the winner. Claude Hopkins used coded coupons to test ads in the early 1900s, and Dan Siroker's tests for the Obama campaign raised sign-ups about 40 percent before he co-founded Optimizely.

Try it with email subject lines, budgeting methods or daily routines. Change one thing at a time, measure what happens, and give it enough time to matter. Just don't let small tests distract from bigger questions.

name: Back-of-the-Envelope Calculation
one_liner: A rough answer in five minutes often beats a precise one next month.
teaser:
A Back-of-the-Envelope Calculation is a fast, rough estimate using simple assumptions and basic arithmetic. It does not aim for precision, only for the right ballpark, so you can quickly see whether an idea, claim or plan makes sense.

Use it to test bold claims at work, total up the real cost of big purchases, and break personal goals into manageable numbers. When the stakes are high, treat it as a starting point and check your assumptions.

name: Cost-Benefit Analysis
one_liner: Count everything a choice will cost and everything it will give, not just what is easy to see.
teaser:
Cost-Benefit Analysis lists the costs and benefits of a decision in comparable terms and asks whether the gains outweigh the price. The tricky part is spotting hidden items, like repairs and resale value, or benefits to people who never pay you.

Use it before big purchases, projects or commitments: write both columns, put rough numbers on each, and include what's easy to forget. Just remember some values resist numbers, and estimates can be wrong.

name: Decision Tree
one_liner: Draw your choices as branches, and the questions that really matter come into view.
teaser:
A Decision Tree lays out each choice, what might happen next and the likely payoff as branches. At Chicago's Cook County Hospital, Lee Goldman's simple tree identified heart attacks more accurately than doctors' judgement, and Chevron uses decision trees for multibillion-dollar investments.

Sketch a quick tree for job offers or warranties, add rough probabilities, and look for the uncertainty that matters most. Or create simple if-then rules for health. Keep trees simple, because they're only as good as their inputs.

name: Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility
one_liner: Each extra helping of a good thing gives you a little less than the one before.
teaser:
Diminishing marginal utility explains why the first glass of water to a thirsty person is precious and the fifth barely matters. Each extra unit of the same thing adds less value, which is why Spotify stopped relying on simply adding more songs and built features that created new kinds of value.

Before acquiring more of something, ask how much the next unit will truly add. When returns in one area flatten, shift time, money, or effort to where it will make a bigger difference. Learn to notice the point where more stops making you meaningfully better off.

name: Opportunity Costs
one_liner: The true price of any choice is the best thing you gave up to make it.
teaser:
Opportunity Costs are the value of the next best alternative you give up when you decide. Every yes is quietly a no to something else, whether that is time, money, energy or attention.

Instead of comparing an option with doing nothing, compare it with the best other use of the same resources. Price your meetings in hours per year, weigh purchases against real alternatives, and protect time for the people who matter.

name: Pro-Con List
one_liner: Getting reasons onto paper, and weighing them, beats juggling them in your head.
teaser:
A pro-con list puts the arguments for and against a decision on paper so you can see them all at once. Benjamin Franklin's version, his moral or prudential algebra, added two upgrades: collect reasons over several days, and strike out items of equal weight.

To use it, give big decisions time, score items instead of counting them, and share lists with the people a choice affects. Watch for bias and gut feelings the list misses. Treat it as a conversation, not a verdict.

name: Sensitivity Analysis
one_liner: Not all assumptions are equal: find the few that swing the whole result.
teaser:
Sensitivity Analysis is the study of how changes in a model's inputs affect its outputs. By adjusting one assumption at a time, such as costs, growth or interest rates, you discover which ones barely matter and which can swing the whole result, as rising costs and delays did at Hinkley Point C.

To use it, stress test big financial decisions at higher interest rates, identify the assumptions your projects depend on most, and build plans that still work when one thing goes wrong.

name: Utilitarianism
one_liner: Judge an action by its consequences for everyone it touches.
teaser:
Utilitarianism judges actions by their consequences. The right choice is the one that produces the greatest overall happiness, or the least suffering, for everyone affected, rather than following fixed rules.

Use it when decisions touch many people: family plans, charitable giving, workplace trade-offs. Count everyone, not just yourself. But add guardrails. Happiness is hard to measure, predictions can be wrong, and adding up benefits can hide serious harm to a few. Pair it with fairness and honesty.

name: Utility Values
one_liner: Value lives in the person, not the object, so the same thing is worth different amounts to different people.
teaser:
Utility value is the personal satisfaction or benefit someone gets from something, which is why two people can value the same item very differently. Tulip bulbs once meant status to some and mere flowers to others, and Dyson charges a premium because buyers value its design and story, not just suction.

Before buying, ask how much genuine benefit something will bring you, not what others think or what it costs. Remember your values will change over time. In negotiations and gift-giving, find out what the other person truly values; differences in value open room for good trades.

name: Veil of Ignorance
one_liner: Write the rules as if you did not know which seat you would get.
teaser:
The Veil of Ignorance, made famous by philosopher John Rawls, asks you to choose rules without knowing whether you'll be rich or poor, boss or newest hire. Because you can't tilt the outcome toward yourself, you're pushed toward choices that feel fair from every position.

Use it when setting work rotas, splitting household chores, or judging local policies. Ask: would I accept this if I drew the worst seat? It won't settle every detail, but it is a sharp test of fairness versus convenience.

name: Discount Rate
one_liner: How much the future counts today depends on one number, and small changes in it flip big decisions.
teaser:
The Discount Rate converts future costs and benefits into present value. A higher rate makes distant outcomes count for less, which is why the Stern Review's very low rate pointed to urgent climate action, and why rising interest rates in 2022 hit startups with far-off profits.

Use it to make your own assumptions visible: automate savings so your future self gets a vote, picture long-term health costs vividly, and test whether decisions survive a different rate.

name: Inflation
one_liner: Money quietly loses value over time, so plans set in fixed amounts slowly shrink.
teaser:
Inflation is the gradual rise in prices that erodes what money can buy. Like a slow leak in a tire, it is easy to ignore until the damage adds up, and in extreme cases such as 1920s Germany it can upend daily life. It also shapes how businesses price, as with Costco's long-held $1.50 hot dog.

Think in real purchasing power rather than nominal amounts. Raise savings goals over time, seek cost-of-living adjustments in long contracts, and remember that money promised years from now is worth less than money today. Grow your skills and value faster than prices rise.

name: Net Present Value
one_liner: Money has a timestamp: compare what something costs today with what its future returns are worth today.
teaser:
Net Present Value converts future cash flows into today's money by discounting them for time, risk and the returns you could earn elsewhere. If what you get back, in today's terms, exceeds what you pay, the investment creates value.

Use it for courses, home upgrades or any choice where costs come now and benefits come later. Be honest about your forecasts and your discount rate, because a precise number can hide hopeful guesses.

name: Switching Costs
one_liner: The effort of changing keeps people where they are, even when something better exists.
teaser:
Switching costs are everything you lose when you change suppliers, systems or habits: fees, effort, learning, data and risk. They explain why people and companies often stay with options that are no longer the best.

Before signing up for anything, check how hard it would be to leave. Notice when hassle, not happiness, is keeping you in place. And raise the cost of slipping back into bad habits to protect the good ones.

name: Counterfactual Thinking
one_liner: To know what made a difference, ask what would have happened without it.
teaser:
Counterfactual Thinking means imagining how events would have unfolded if one factor had been different. It is the only way to judge whether a decision, product or habit really made a difference, or whether the result would have happened anyway.

Use it by finding a comparison: a month, region or person without the change. Test by removal, pausing something to see what shifts. And use balanced what-ifs to put regrets in perspective.

name: Exit Strategy
one_liner: The best time to plan your way out is before you go in.
teaser:
An Exit Strategy is a plan for leaving an investment, market or commitment: the conditions that trigger it, how you'll do it, and how you'll protect what you've built. At Gallipoli, a carefully planned withdrawal got over 100,000 troops out with very few casualties.

Use it before you start anything uncertain: write your stop and continue criteria, set money rules while calm, and build review points into commitments. Revisit the plan as facts change.

name: OODA Loop
one_liner: Whoever observes, makes sense, decides and acts faster can adapt while others are still catching up.
teaser:
The OODA Loop, developed by fighter pilot John Boyd, is a decision cycle: Observe what is happening, Orient by making sense of it, Decide on a response and Act, then loop again. Whoever cycles faster adapts while others are still catching up.

Use it to shorten feedback cycles at work, run small weekly experiments with your health and pause to orient before reacting in conflict. Move quickly, but keep checking that your view of the world is accurate.

name: Second-Order Thinking
one_liner: Every action has consequences, and those consequences have consequences of their own.
teaser:
Second/Third Order Thinking means asking what happens next, and then after that. First-order effects are the obvious results we intend. Second- and third-order effects are the reactions, and the reactions to the reactions, which often decide whether a choice succeeds or backfires.

Before a big decision, trace at least two steps ahead. Ask how people, systems and habits will respond, and whether today's fix creates tomorrow's problem. Use it most where choices affect others, but don't let it paralyse small decisions.

name: Thought Experiment
one_liner: Careful imagination can test an idea before it costs you anything.
teaser:
A Thought Experiment is a mental exercise where you imagine a situation and reason through what would happen. By changing a detail, pushing an idea to its extreme or seeing through someone else's eyes, you can expose contradictions and options that ordinary thinking misses.

Use it before costly decisions. Ask what a fresh stranger would do in your role, imagine owning a purchase for a year, or picture a fair friend hearing both sides of an argument. Then check your conclusions against real evidence.

name: Analysis Paralysis
one_liner: Waiting for perfect information can cost more than acting on good enough.
teaser:
Analysis Paralysis is when overthinking a decision stops you from acting at all, often driven by fear of choosing wrong and the false belief that more information always helps. Nokia built smartphone prototypes but stalled in endless analysis while Apple and Android reshaped the market.

Decide small things instantly rather than deliberating. For bigger choices, set a firm decision deadline and act with what you know when it arrives. Aim for roughly 70% confidence instead of certainty, and remember that most decisions are reversible: imperfect action often beats perfect inaction.

name: False Dilemma
one_liner: When a choice is framed as either-or, the best option is often the one nobody mentioned.
teaser:
A False Dilemma presents a decision as if only two options exist, when more are available. It feels decisive, but it stops us searching. Kennedy rejected air strikes versus doing nothing in 1962, and IKEA refused to choose between cheap and well designed.

When you hear either-or language, pause and list a third and fourth option before choosing. Be wary of urgency that forces a binary. But stay honest: some choices really are yes or no.

name: Grey Thinking
one_liner: Most important questions have no clean right side, and the best answers often sit between the extremes.
teaser:
Grey Thinking means accepting that most important issues involve trade-offs and uncertainty rather than a clear right and wrong side. It looks for solutions in the middle ground that binary debates ignore.

To practise it, state the strongest version of the other view before your own, swap yes-or-no questions for how-much questions, and think in probabilities rather than certainties. Some issues are black and white, but most are not.

name: Hick’s Law
one_liner: The more options you face, the longer it takes to choose.
teaser:
Hick's Law states that the time it takes to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices available. Every extra option adds mental load, which is why a short menu is easier to order from than a twenty-page one. Simpler choices often lead to faster, better decisions.

Reduce routine choices with simple systems such as a meal plan or a capsule wardrobe. Break big decisions into smaller steps, and narrow your options to a shortlist before deep analysis. If you design products or messages, give people fewer, clearer options.

name: Information Overload
one_liner: Past a certain point, more information buries the one signal that matters.
teaser:
Information Overload happens when the volume of information exceeds our ability to process it. Decisions slow down, stress rises, and the one warning that matters gets lost among dozens that don't, as with the ignored radar report at Pearl Harbor or Equifax's unapplied patch.

To use it, decide in advance which signals deserve your attention and silence the rest. Cap your research before big choices, limit news to one trusted source, and review your filters regularly so critical warnings still get through.

name: Paradox of Choice
one_liner: Some choice makes us free; too much choice makes us anxious and less satisfied.
teaser:
The paradox of choice, popularised by psychologist Barry Schwartz, is the idea that while some choice is good, too much can lead to anxiety, decision paralysis and less satisfaction with what we pick. In a well-known jam study, shoppers offered six flavours were far more likely to buy than those offered twenty-four.

Limit options where they don't matter, for example with a smaller wardrobe or a simple rule like always booking the mid-priced option. For important choices, set your criteria first and settle for an option that clearly meets them rather than chasing the perfect one.

name: Satisficing
one_liner: Set a bar for good enough, and stop searching when something clears it.
teaser:
Satisficing, a word coined by Herbert Simon, means setting a bar for good enough and choosing the first option that clears it. Because our time, information and attention are limited, chasing the perfect choice often costs more than it gains.

To use it, define your must-have criteria before you start looking, then stop at the first option that meets them. Save exhaustive searching for high-stakes decisions like hiring, health or major investments.

name: Tendency to Want to Do Something
one_liner: We feel driven to act, even when waiting would serve us better.
teaser:
The Tendency to Want to do Something is our powerful drive to take action, even when patience would serve us better. Action feels productive while waiting feels weak, so we tinker and intervene, sometimes making things worse, as Rome learned at Cannae and frequent traders learn from their returns.

To use it, write down your plans in advance, pause before reacting at work, and let simple problems resolve on their own. Inaction is also a choice. Act when it truly helps, not just to ease anxiety.

episode.title: Tendency to Want to do Something

name: Burn the Boats
one_liner: Removing the way back can turn a hesitant effort into total commitment.
teaser:
Burn the Boats means removing your escape routes so the only way forward is success. The phrase comes from Hernán Cortés, who in 1519 scuttled his ships in Mexico so his men could not turn back. Without a fallback, focus and commitment sharpen dramatically.

Use it selectively for goals that need total commitment. Remove easy exits by prepaying, deleting distractions, or giving away what tempts you back to old habits. Make public commitments to add accountability, but save this approach for choices you are truly ready to go all in on.

name: Circle of Competence
one_liner: Knowing where your knowledge ends matters more than how far it reaches.
teaser:
The Circle of Competence is the area where your knowledge is deep enough to judge decisions well. Its size matters less than knowing exactly where its boundary lies, because confidence outside it is dangerous.

Before a big investment or career move, ask whether you could explain the key risks in plain words. If not, study more, ask an expert or step back. Grow your circle with small, low-cost experiments.

name: Devil’s Advocate Position
one_liner: An idea worth backing should survive someone arguing hard against it.
teaser:
The devil's advocate position means arguing against a plan or belief on purpose, not because you oppose it, but to expose weak assumptions. The name comes from the Catholic Church official who argued against candidates for sainthood.

Use it when stakes are high and agreement comes too easily. Assign the role, rotate it so no one becomes the permanent critic, and make the case against your own big decisions before you commit.

episode.title: Devil's Advocate: The Art of Constructive Contrarianism

name: Nuclear Option
one_liner: The most extreme move can settle a fight, but its damage may outlast the problem it solved.
teaser:
The Nuclear Option is an extreme move that resolves a situation definitively but causes damage that can't be undone. Sherman's March to the Sea helped end the Civil War yet left lasting resentment. Used well, it can also change the game, as IBM's open PC architecture did.

Before an irreversible decision, like quitting dramatically or ending a relationship over one issue, weigh all the fallout. Exhaust less drastic options first. Sometimes simply having the extreme option available is enough to shift a situation without ever using it.

name: Pyrrhic Victory
one_liner: A win that costs too much can leave you worse off than losing.
teaser:
A Pyrrhic Victory is a win that drains the winner. The British took Bunker Hill in 1775 but lost nearly half their attackers, and RBS won the bidding war for ABN AMRO just before the financial crisis, then needed a huge government rescue.

Use it by counting the full cost before you fight: in arguments, ask what winning does to the relationship; in deals, set a walk-away point; and in big pushes at work, make sure you'll still be standing after the finish line.

name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
one_liner: What you have already spent is gone, so it should not decide what you do next.
teaser:
The Sunk Cost Fallacy is sticking with a project because of the money, time or effort already spent, even when the future looks poor. Britain and France kept funding Concorde as costs soared, and Airbus built the A380 for years after orders dried up.

Judge each decision as if starting fresh: is the next hour or dollar worth spending? Persistence can be wise, but stay because of what is ahead, not because of what is behind.

episode.title: Sunk Cost Fallacy: When Cutting Our Losses Seems Like Losing

name: Winner’s Curse
one_liner: In a contest over an uncertain prize, the winner is often whoever overestimated it most.
teaser:
The Winner's Curse happens when many bidders estimate an uncertain value. Their guesses scatter around the truth, and the highest guess wins, so the winner is often the person who overestimated the most.

Before any bidding war, whether for a house, a candidate or a company, set your walk-away price while you're calm. If you win easily or by a mile, ask what you might have missed, and be willing to let someone else overpay.

name: Expected Value
one_liner: A choice is worth its average result across all the ways it could turn out.
teaser:
Expected value is what a decision is worth on average if you could repeat it many times. Multiply each possible outcome by its probability and add them up. It lets you compare choices on their long-run merits rather than on hope or fear.

To use it, check whether offers like warranties are worth their price, and take small bets with big upsides. But remember its limits: it assumes many tries and treats every dollar alike, so when ruin is possible, weigh survival first.

name: Fat-Tailed Distributions
one_liner: In some areas, extreme events are far more common than the bell curve says.
teaser:
In fat-tailed distributions, extreme outcomes are far more common than a bell curve suggests, so a few events can dominate the average. Wealth, market returns, city sizes, and book sales work this way, and risk models that assumed normal distributions underestimated the 2008 financial crisis.

When dealing with fat-tailed domains, plan for worst cases that are worse and more likely than they seem, and be wary of averages. On the upside, small bets with uncapped potential, in careers, investments, or creative work, can pay off far beyond what typical outcomes suggest.

name: Foxes vs Hedgehogs
one_liner: Some minds know many things, others one big thing, and each has its blind spot.
teaser:
Foxes vs. Hedgehogs, from Isaiah Berlin's famous essay, contrasts two thinking styles. Foxes know many things and adapt to each situation. Hedgehogs know one big thing and see the world through a single unifying idea.

Think like a fox when forecasting or making sense of something complex, gathering several perspectives. Act like a hedgehog when pursuing a long-term goal, keeping one priority in focus.

name: Law of Large Numbers
one_liner: Luck is wild in small samples and predictable in large ones.
teaser:
The law of large numbers says that as a random process is repeated many times, the average result settles toward its true expected value. Small samples are noisy and can mislead, while large samples are reliable. It is why casinos and bookmakers profit steadily from small margins.

To use it, be patient with early results, skeptical of single stories, and trust patterns built from many observations. But remember it does not mean a losing streak is due to end, and it cannot fix biased data.

name: Lindy Effect
one_liner: For things that do not wear out, every year survived predicts more years to come.
teaser:
The Lindy Effect says that for books, ideas, technologies and institutions, past survival predicts future survival. A book read for a century will likely outlast this year's bestseller, because every year it lasts is evidence of hidden strength.

Use it to choose what to learn, which habits to adopt and which tools to rely on. Give proven classics more weight than fads. Just remember it applies to non-perishable things, not people or machines, and it is a rule of thumb, not a guarantee.

name: Monte Carlo Simulation
one_liner: When odds are too tangled to calculate, play the future many times and count.
teaser:
Monte Carlo simulation uses random sampling to estimate outcomes that are too complex to calculate directly. You model the uncertain inputs, run the scenario thousands of times, and see how often each result occurs. The answer is a picture of probabilities rather than a single forecast.

To use it, ask what happens across many possible versions of the future, not just the best guess. Check your savings odds, plan projects around realistic runs, and remember a simulation is only as good as its assumptions.

name: Prediction Market
one_liner: When people must pay for being wrong, their forecasts get sharper.
teaser:
A prediction market pays out depending on whether an event happens. If a one-dollar contract trades at sixty cents, the crowd sees about a sixty percent chance. Because wrong traders lose money, prices tend to blend scattered information into useful forecasts.

Borrow the idea: ask your team for anonymous probabilities, put numbers on your own predictions and check them later. Treat market odds as one input, not gospel, since thin markets can be swayed.

name: Probabilistic Thinking
one_liner: The future is a spread of possible outcomes, each with its own odds.
teaser:
Probabilistic Thinking means thinking in odds instead of certainties. Rather than asking whether something will happen, you ask how likely it is and what follows in each case, weighing options by their expected value.

Use it by putting rough numbers on predictions, tracking how often you are right, thinking in odds about health risks and judging money choices by their quality, not just their outcomes. Treat estimates as best guesses and update them as evidence arrives.

name: Randomness
one_liner: Much of life is chance, and our minds invent patterns that are not there.
teaser:
Randomness means individual outcomes can't be predicted, yet we keep spotting patterns in pure chance. Britain built ERNIE in 1957 to pick Premium Bond winners from electrical noise, while EA's random FIFA packs earned billions and were ruled illegal gambling in Belgium.

Before reacting to a streak, check whether it's noise. Set budgets before buying anything sold as a lucky dip. And use a coin flip on purpose when you need a fair, unrigged decision.

name: Super Forecasters
one_liner: Good prediction comes less from genius than from habits anyone can learn.
teaser:
Super Forecasters consistently beat the crowd at predicting events. Philip Tetlock collected tens of thousands of expert forecasts and found most barely beat chance, but open-minded foxes did better than one-idea hedgehogs. Metaculus now scores forecasters and weights the best.

To forecast better, put numbers on your predictions, write them down and check them, update gradually with new evidence, and consider several explanations. Even the best are often wrong, but keeping score makes you less wrong over time.

name: Availability Bias
one_liner: What comes to mind easily feels likely, whether or not it is.
teaser:
Availability bias makes recent, vivid or emotional events feel more common than they are, while quieter risks fade from view. It shapes what we fear, insure against and pay attention to.

Counter it by checking frightening headlines against real rates, setting up insurance and savings based on actual risk rather than recent news, and reviewing the full record before judging people or projects by their latest moment.

name: Conjunction Fallacy
one_liner: Every added detail makes a story more convincing and less likely.
teaser:
The conjunction fallacy happens when a detailed story feels more probable than a simpler one. Every added condition can only keep the odds the same or lower them, yet vivid detail makes outcomes feel more believable.

When a plan, forecast or worry depends on several things happening together, list each assumption and estimate it separately. Remember that the combined chance is always lower than its weakest single link.

name: Gambler’s Fallacy
one_liner: Chance keeps no score, so nothing is ever due.
teaser:
The Gambler's Fallacy is the belief that a streak makes the opposite outcome more likely, or that a rare result is due. For independent events, like coin flips and lottery draws, the past has no influence. When number 53 went missing from Italy's Venice lottery for 182 draws, Italians bet billions on it anyway.

Use it whenever you feel something is overdue: check whether the events are truly independent, judge each case on its merits, and look at reasons, not runs.

name: Hot-Hand Fallacy
one_liner: A winning streak feels like momentum, but it is often luck on a good run.
teaser:
The Hot-Hand Fallacy is believing a winning streak makes the next win more likely. A famous 1985 basketball study found streaks looked like chance, though later work suggests a small effect. ARK Invest's fund soared in 2020, but much of the money arrived after the run, and many investors lost.

When something has been winning lately, ask what is driving it and whether those causes still hold. Set your plan in advance so a streak doesn't make the decision for you.

episode.title: Hot Hand Fallacy: When Streaks Deceive

name: Monte Carlo Fallacy
one_liner: A roulette wheel has no memory, however long the streak.
teaser:
The Monte Carlo Fallacy, or gambler's fallacy, is the belief that a run of one result makes the opposite more likely next time. But independent events like coin tosses and roulette spins have no memory.

When you catch yourself thinking something is due, ask whether the events are truly independent. If they are, the streak means nothing. If they aren't, like health or job performance, look for the real cause.

name: Mr Market
one_liner: The market is a moody partner: use its offers, never its moods.
teaser:
Mr. Market is Benjamin Graham's picture of the stock market as a moody business partner who offers to buy or sell every day at prices driven by emotion rather than value. In fearful moments, such as the 1938 recession or the March 2020 crash, prices can fall far below what assets are worth.

Treat Mr. Market's quotes as offers you are free to ignore, not instructions. Do your own analysis of value, keep a list of quality assets you would like to own, and act only when price and value diverge in your favor. Stay calm when others are euphoric or panicked.

name: Prospect Theory
one_liner: Losses hurt about twice as much as equal gains please, and that bends our choices.
teaser:
Prospect Theory, from Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, explains how we really make risky choices. We judge outcomes as gains or losses from a reference point, feel losses more sharply than equal gains, and take reckless risks to escape a loss.

Use it by reframing decisions both ways to see if your preference flips, resisting the urge to break even on a losing bet, and harnessing loss aversion to keep good habits on track.

name: Black Swan Event
one_liner: What matters most is often what nobody saw coming.
teaser:
A Black Swan, popularised by Nassim Nicholas Taleb, is a rare and unforeseeable event with enormous consequences, named after the black swans Europeans once thought impossible. Events like 9/11 and COVID-19 show the limits of predicting the future from past data.

Since you can't predict Black Swans, build for them instead. Stay humble about forecasts, diversify your skills and investments, keep backup plans and redundancy for critical systems, and aim for antifragility: positioning yourself to withstand shocks and even benefit from them.

name: Boiling Frog
one_liner: The most dangerous changes are often the slowest ones.
teaser:
The Boiling Frog describes how gradual change slips past our alarms. Each small step feels normal compared to yesterday, so people and organisations stay put while conditions get steadily worse.

To use it, compare today against a fixed reference point, like last year, not last week. Set tripwires in advance that trigger action when crossed, and review your health, money and relationships regularly.

name: Butterfly Effect
one_liner: In a complex system, a tiny change at the start can grow into a huge difference at the end.
teaser:
The Butterfly Effect is the idea that in complex systems, very small changes at the start can grow into enormous differences later. It's why long-range weather forecasts break down.

Use it two ways. Stay humble about long-term predictions and write your plans in pencil. And respect small actions: a slightly earlier alarm, a brief thank-you or a careful word can compound into outcomes far larger than they first appear.

name: Chaos Theory
one_liner: Some systems follow exact rules yet still cannot be predicted far ahead.
teaser:
Chaos Theory studies systems that follow precise rules yet become unpredictable over time, because tiny differences in starting conditions keep growing. Chaos isn't randomness; it's order too intricate to forecast far ahead.

Use it to plan for surprises instead of predictions. Keep emergency buffers, shorten feedback loops at work, and build slack into busy family calendars. Trust short-term forecasts more than long-term ones, and adapt as you go.

name: Murphy’s Law
one_liner: If something can go wrong, given enough time and people, it eventually will.
teaser:
Murphy's Law states that anything that can go wrong will go wrong. It's not literal pessimism, but a reminder that with enough time and repetition, every possible mistake eventually happens.

Use it by rolling out changes in stages, building backups for travel and money, and designing your home and work so errors are hard to make. Focus on the failures that are most likely or most damaging, since you can't prepare for everything.

name: Peak
one_liner: Most rises top out, and the top is the hardest place to see it from.
teaser:
A peak is the highest point of something, the moment a rising trend turns downward. Resources, products, companies and career phases all tend to top out eventually, and the peak rarely announces itself. From the top, everything looks its best just before it gets worse.

To use it, prepare for transitions while things are going well. Learn new skills when your role feels easiest, question assets that seem destined to rise forever, and schedule hard work for your daily energy peaks. But peaks are not always final: new methods can create fresh highs.

name: Unknown Unknowns
one_liner: The biggest risks are often the ones missing from your list.
teaser:
Unknown Unknowns are the factors we are not even aware we are missing. Unlike known unknowns, the open questions we can name, they sit completely outside our list of risks, so no forecast includes them.

You can't predict them, but you can prepare. Build buffers like emergency savings and spare time in schedules. Ask outsiders to find blind spots in your plans. Strengthen general resilience in your health and work, so whatever surprise arrives, you can absorb it and recover.

name: Antifragility
one_liner: Some things break under stress, some resist it, and some grow stronger from it.
teaser:
Fragile things break under stress, robust things resist it, and antifragile things improve because of it. The idea helps us design careers, finances and organisations that survive surprises and sometimes profit from them.

To use it, keep most of your life safe, take small risks with big upside, build adaptable skills, and welcome small doses of stress with time to recover.

name: De-Risking
one_liner: You can keep most of the upside while cutting the risk of ruin.
teaser:
De-risking means reducing the uncertainty and potential downside of a decision while keeping its upside. It is not about avoiding risk altogether, but about managing it through diversification, hedging, testing and backup plans. Medieval Venetian traders spread capital across ships so no single loss could ruin them.

Before a big move, identify what could go wrong and how badly. Spread your bets, test ideas on a small scale before committing fully, and build buffers such as savings or backup options. Aim to make your downside survivable while leaving room for upside.

name: Margin of Safety
one_liner: Build in a buffer, so that being wrong is not a catastrophe.
teaser:
A margin of safety is extra capacity built in because forecasts, materials and people are imperfect. The Brooklyn Bridge's cables were designed roughly six times stronger than needed and survived faulty wire. Fukushima's sea wall was sized for the expected tsunami, not the possible one.

To use it, keep an emergency fund, pad your deadlines, and leave slack in your schedule. Size the buffer to the stakes, and ask not just what's likely but what's possible.

name: Moral Hazard
one_liner: People take bigger risks when someone else will pay if things go wrong.
teaser:
Moral Hazard is the tendency to take on more risk when you are shielded from the consequences. Insurance, guarantees and bailouts are useful, but they can quietly change behavior when the decision maker keeps the upside and someone else absorbs the downside.

Whenever you design incentives, offer help or accept a guarantee, ask who pays if it fails. Keep authority and responsibility together, and make sure risk-takers keep some skin in the game.

name: Preserving Optionality
one_liner: When the future is unclear, the right to choose later is worth paying for.
teaser:
Preserving Optionality is the strategy of keeping choices open so you can adapt when circumstances change. Instead of committing everything early, you make small, affordable moves that give you the right to act later, like Thales securing olive presses with small deposits before a harvest.

To use it, build skills that work in many fields, keep an emergency fund, and test big life choices before committing. Just remember that at some point, you need to pick a path and commit.

name: Resilience
one_liner: Setbacks are certain; collapse is not, if you prepare to recover.
teaser:
Resilience is the ability to bounce back and adapt in the face of adversity. It isn't about avoiding hardship, but absorbing the blow and finding a way forward, as Shackleton did when he brought all his men home from Antarctica, or Maersk did rebuilding its network in about ten days.

To use it, build backups before you need them, invest in routines and relationships that steady you, and keep a financial cushion. Remember that resilience needs rest too.

name: Scenario Analysis
one_liner: Rehearse several futures, so whichever one arrives feels familiar.
teaser:
Scenario Analysis means sketching a handful of distinct, plausible futures, such as a boom, a bust and a surprise, then working out how each would affect your plans. The aim is not to predict correctly but to make change feel familiar instead of shocking.

Use it for big, uncertain decisions: a job move, a budget, a major event. Ask what you would do in each scenario and look for steps that help in all of them. Keep it to three or four vivid stories so planning leads to action.

name: Stop the Bleeding
one_liner: When losses mount, halt them first and plan the recovery after.
teaser:
Stop the Bleeding is the principle that when things go wrong, your first job is to halt further losses before attempting a comeback. Stabilise first, then rebuild.

Use it at the first sign of a spiral: cut unused spending before planning a recovery, freeze a failing project before adding people, and pause a heated argument before trying to resolve it. But don't cut so deep that you damage what you'll need to recover.

name: Frame of Reference
one_liner: Every judgement is measured against something; change the baseline and the answer can change.
teaser:
In physics, a frame of reference is the coordinate system used to describe motion. A cup on an airplane tray is still to the passenger but racing relative to the ground. In life, every judgment of value, progress or fairness depends on the baseline we choose, and changing the baseline can flip the conclusion.

To use it, test important judgments against two or three different baselines. Price big purchases by cost per use, compare your progress with your past self, and in disagreements ask what the other person is measuring against. Watch out for reframing used to manipulate.

name: High Context vs Low Context
one_liner: Some cultures put the meaning in the words; others leave it in the relationship and the silence.
teaser:
Anthropologist Edward T. Hall distinguished high-context cultures, such as Japan and China, where meaning lives in relationships, tone, and shared understanding, from low-context cultures, such as the US and Germany, where people say exactly what they mean. Misreading the style causes many cross-cultural misunderstandings.

Notice your own default style and how it might land with others. Learn the context of colleagues and partners: an indirect answer may be a polite 'no', while bluntness may simply be clarity. Listen beyond the words to the relationships and norms around them.

name: Introverts vs Extroverts
one_liner: People differ in where they find their energy, and good teams make room for both kinds.
teaser:
Introversion and extroversion describe where people tend to draw their energy. Introverts often recharge in solitude and prefer deeper one-to-one conversation, while extroverts tend to gain energy from people and activity. Most of us sit somewhere in between.

Use it to design meetings that suit both styles, such as sharing agendas early and collecting written ideas, to respect different recharge needs in relationships, and to plan your own energy so you avoid burnout.

name: IQ vs EQ
one_liner: Being clever and being wise with people are different strengths, and big decisions need both.
teaser:
IQ, or intelligence quotient, measures cognitive skills like reasoning and problem solving. EQ, or emotional intelligence, describes how well we recognise and manage emotions in ourselves and others. They are different strengths, and the best decisions often need both.

To build EQ, name your feelings before reacting, respond to the emotion behind people's words, and ask for feedback on how you come across, not just whether you were right.

name: Language Instinct
one_liner: Children are born ready for language, and some abilities grow best through use, not drills.
teaser:
The Language Instinct, popularised by Steven Pinker, is the idea that humans are born ready to acquire language. Children absorb grammar from messy everyday speech, and deaf children in Nicaragua even invented a full sign language that no adult taught them.

To use it, favour immersion and real conversation over memorisation when learning a skill. Talk richly with children, and remember that groups absorb unspoken rules the way kids absorb grammar, so model the behaviour you want to see.

name: Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs
one_liner: Unmet basic needs drown out higher ones, so check the foundations before blaming motivation.
teaser:
Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs, proposed by Abraham Maslow in 1943, suggests our motivations move through levels: physiological, safety, love and belonging, esteem and self-actualization. When basic needs go unmet, they crowd out higher goals.

Use it to diagnose low moods by checking sleep, food and safety first, to help friends with practical worries before big dreams, and to lead teams by caring for every level. Treat it as a lens, not a strict ladder.

name: Peak-end Rule
one_liner: We remember an experience by its most intense moment and its ending, not by its length.
teaser:
The Peak-end Rule describes how we remember experiences. Instead of averaging every minute, our memory focuses on the most intense moment, good or bad, and on how things ended, while largely ignoring duration.

Use it to design better experiences. End work days with a satisfying task, finish workouts gently, and close disagreements with warmth. Invest in a few memorable highs and graceful endings. Just remember that steady everyday quality still matters, even if memory overlooks it.

name: Theory of Mind
one_liner: Other people act on what they know and believe, not on what you know.
teaser:
Theory of mind is the ability to recognise that other people have their own beliefs, desires and emotions, and to predict what they will do based on what they know, not what you know. Psychologists test it with tasks like the Sally-Anne false-belief test.

Use it before important conversations: ask what the other person knows, wants and fears. Explain ideas from your listener's starting point, and treat your guesses about others as hypotheses to check.

name: False Consensus Effect
one_liner: We think far more people share our views and choices than really do.
teaser:
The false consensus effect is our tendency to assume others share our opinions, preferences, and choices more than they do. In a classic 1977 Stanford study, students who agreed or refused to wear a sign around campus both overestimated how many peers would choose as they did.

Before assuming others agree, ask how someone with different experiences might see it. Widen your information sources and social circles so your sense of normal stays calibrated. When a decision depends on what others want, ask open questions or gather real data instead of relying on intuition.

name: Fundamental Attribution Error
one_liner: We blame people’s character for their behaviour and forget the situation pushing them.
teaser:
The fundamental attribution error is our habit of explaining others' actions by personality, such as lazy, rude or dishonest, while overlooking the pressures and circumstances around them. Ironically, we excuse our own mistakes by pointing to the situation.

To counter it, ask what situation might explain a behavior before judging the person. At work, check incentives, workload and systems first, because fixing the setup often fixes the behavior.

name: Halo Effect
one_liner: One shining quality makes us rate everything else about a person or product higher.
teaser:
The halo effect is our tendency to let one positive trait colour our judgement of everything else about a person, product or brand. Psychologist Edward Thorndike found that officers who rated soldiers well on one quality tended to rate them well on unrelated ones. One shining quality can hide real weaknesses.

Judge qualities separately: use a scorecard with distinct criteria rather than an overall impression. When you are impressed by someone or something, deliberately look for drawbacks, and for important decisions like hiring, use structured evaluations that keep one standout trait from deciding everything.

name: Hanlon’s Razor
one_liner: Never put down to malice what can be explained by mistake, muddle or accident.
teaser:
Hanlon's Razor tells us to assume mistakes before malice. When something goes wrong, the cause is usually an error, a misunderstanding or a broken process, not a deliberate plot, and assuming bad intent leads to anger and the wrong fixes.

To use it, ask neutral questions before accusing, look for system failures first, and stay calm with colleagues, companies and loved ones. But watch for repeated patterns that do suggest intent.

name: Horn Effect
one_liner: One bad impression can cast a shadow over everything else we see in someone.
teaser:
The Horn Effect is the opposite of the halo effect. One negative detail, such as a bad first impression or a single mistake, spills over and makes unrelated qualities seem worse than they really are.

To counter it, evaluate traits separately, give people a second look, and judge products by the features that actually matter to you. Take genuine red flags seriously, but don't let one blemish rewrite the whole picture.

name: In-Group Favouritism
one_liner: We give more trust, help and reward to people we see as our own, even when the group means nothing.
teaser:
In-group favoritism is our tendency to give more trust, help and rewards to people we see as one of us. Henri Tajfel showed it appears even when groups are based on something trivial, like a preference for one painter over another.

To counter it, use structured, blind or independent scoring for hiring and promotions, build shared goals that bring groups together, and test your judgments by asking how you would react if a rival did the same thing.

name: Most Respectable Interpretation
one_liner: Read other people’s words in the most reasonable light first; the harshest reading is rarely right.
teaser:
The Most Respectable Interpretation is the habit of reading others' words and actions in the most reasonable and charitable way possible. Our first reading is often our least generous, and good faith keeps conversations open and prevents needless conflict.

When a message stings, pause, think of two generous explanations, and ask a curious question before reacting. Stay charitable, but let repeated evidence of bad faith update your view.

name: Out-Group Bias
one_liner: We judge outsiders more harshly, and a simple team name is enough to start it.
teaser:
Out-group bias is our tendency to view people outside our own group with suspicion, trusting them less and reading their actions in the worst light. Even groups formed minutes ago can trigger it.

To counter it, judge ideas on their merits, not their source. Build shared goals with other groups, and seek out thoughtful voices who see the world differently.

name: Liking and Loving Tendency
one_liner: Once we like someone or something, we overlook its flaws and overrate its merits.
teaser:
The tendency to like or love is our inclination to favour people, products or ideas we associate with positive feelings. It can override objective judgement, leading us to overlook flaws in what we like and discount the merits of what we don't. Brand loyalty can even change how something seems to taste.

Audit your preferences: do you genuinely value this, or do you like it because of what it is associated with? Try explaining your choice to someone with a very different perspective. When stakes are high, ask a neutral person to review decisions involving people or things you love.

name: Anchoring
one_liner: The first number we hear quietly steers every judgement that follows.
teaser:
Anchoring is the bias where an initial number or impression becomes a reference point for later decisions. We adjust away from it, but rarely enough, even when the anchor is arbitrary or chosen by someone else.

To use it wisely, do your research before seeing anyone's first offer, set well-justified anchors yourself, and ask what you'd conclude if you'd never seen the opening figure. Always notice who set the starting point.

name: Backfire Effect
one_liner: Facts thrown at a cherished belief can make people hold it tighter.
teaser:
The Backfire Effect describes how corrections can sometimes strengthen the beliefs they target, especially when those beliefs are tied to identity. Research suggests full backfire is rarer than first thought, but facts alone often fail to persuade.

To change minds, lead with shared goals, ask questions rather than issue verdicts, and offer a better explanation instead of a bare denial. And watch for your own defensiveness too.

name: Bait and Switch
one_liner: An offer built to change once you are committed is not the offer you are buying.
teaser:
Bait and Switch uses an appealing offer to win your attention, then substitutes something less favourable after you've invested time, effort or emotion. It works because walking away feels like wasting what you've already put in.

When a deal changes, ask whether you'd have come for the new version. Get important promises in writing, and be honest about your own asks so you never borrow trust you can't repay.

name: Dark Patterns
one_liner: Design can quietly steer you into choices you never meant to make.
teaser:
Dark Patterns are design techniques that steer people into actions against their interests, like hidden fees, pre-ticked boxes and hard-to-cancel subscriptions. The Columbia Record Club billed members for albums unless they declined in time, and Noom paid about 62 million dollars over hard-to-cancel renewals.

Slow down at checkout, set reminders before trials end, and turn off hook-you notifications. If you design for others, make leaving as easy as joining, and ask whether customers would feel tricked.

name: Framing
one_liner: The same facts can lead to opposite choices, depending on how they are presented.
teaser:
Framing is the way a choice or fact is presented, the words used and what gets emphasised, and it changes how we feel and decide. Ninety percent survival sounds better than ten percent mortality, though they mean the same thing.

Protect yourself by restating offers in the opposite direction before you commit. Communicate better by framing requests around others' goals. And always ask whether a frame informs or manipulates.

name: Nudging
one_liner: Small changes in how choices are arranged can change what people choose, without forbidding anything.
teaser:
Nudging means designing choices so the better option is the easy one. Countries where organ donation is the default have far higher consent, and simply monitoring Virgin Atlantic captains helped them save fuel.

Use it on yourself first: put healthy food at eye level, automate savings on payday, and set up meetings and dinners so good habits happen by default. Keep nudges transparent and easy to opt out of, especially when you're nudging other people.

name: Reciprocity
one_liner: We feel a strong pull to return what we are given, kindness and harm alike.
teaser:
Reciprocity is the principle of give and take. When someone does something for us, we feel compelled to return the favor, sometimes decades later. It underpins trust, trade and friendship across cultures, and it can be used to build goodwill or to manufacture obligation.

To use it, give first: share, introduce and help before you need anything. Keep relationships balanced with small, unprompted gestures. And when a salesperson hands you something free before a pitch, ask whether you'd want the product without the gift. Generous, patient reciprocity works best.

name: Social Proof
one_liner: When we are unsure what to do, we copy what other people are doing.
teaser:
Social Proof is our tendency to follow the behaviour of others, especially in uncertain situations. When we don't know what to do, we assume the crowd knows best, which is why more passers-by stopped to stare up when bigger groups were already looking.

To use it, choose your crowd on purpose to build healthier habits, and question purchases driven purely by hype. When encouraging others, highlight what most people already do. The crowd can be wrong, so treat it as one signal among many.

name: Streisand Effect
one_liner: Trying to hide something often makes far more people look at it.
teaser:
The Streisand Effect is when an attempt to hide, censor or remove information backfires and makes it spread further. The act of suppression becomes a story, and curiosity does the rest.

To use it, answer criticism openly instead of trying to bury it, think before banning or deleting, and ask how your request would look if everyone could see it.

name: Winning Hearts and Minds
one_liner: Lasting support comes from meeting people’s real needs, not from forcing them to comply.
teaser:
Winning Hearts and Minds is a strategy for gaining a population's trust and cooperation by meeting real needs. The heart is emotional goodwill; the mind is a rational belief that siding with you is in their interest.

Use it whenever you need cooperation that lasts. Earn trust before asking for change, link requests to what people value, and give before you ask. Be patient and sincere, because people quickly spot generosity that's only a tactic.

name: Appeasement
one_liner: Giving in to keep the peace can invite bigger demands later.
teaser:
Appeasement is the policy of making concessions to an aggressor in the hope of avoiding conflict. Sometimes it buys time, but when concessions look like weakness, they can encourage further demands, as the Munich Agreement did in 1938.

To use it, notice when giving in to avoid friction creates a pattern. Set clear, polite boundaries early at work, separate generous compromise from silent surrender in relationships, and stay consistent with children. Ask whether a concession solves the problem or just postpones it.

name: Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement
one_liner: Your power in a deal comes from what you will do if the deal fails.
teaser:
Your Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement, or BATNA, is what you will actually do if a deal falls through. The better that alternative, the less you need any one deal and the more calmly you can negotiate.

Before any important negotiation, write down your walk-away option and work to improve it. Get a second quote, a competing offer or a backup plan. Then accept only deals that beat it.

name: Call Your Bluff
one_liner: Many threats are cheaper to make than to carry out, so test them before you fold.
teaser:
Calling a bluff means challenging a threat or claim so the other side has to prove it. The West answered Stalin's Berlin blockade with an airlift, and he backed down without war. Carl Icahn bought into Herbalife against Bill Ackman's huge short, and the company did not collapse.

Test take-it-or-leave-it offers and assumed barriers calmly. But calling a bluff carries risk, so start small, keep an exit open, and make sure you can afford to be wrong.

name: Deterrence
one_liner: A threat that others believe you will carry out can stop a fight before it starts.
teaser:
Deterrence works when others believe you can and will respond. Britain executed Admiral Byng in 1757 partly as a warning to other officers, and American Airlines flooded its Dallas routes with cheap seats until small rivals left.

Use it by making your boundaries credible: enforce them the first time, add visible protections at home and online, and keep consequences proportionate so you'll actually follow through. Threats you never carry out teach people to ignore you.

name: Mutually Assured Destruction
one_liner: When both sides can destroy each other, neither dares to strike first.
teaser:
Mutually Assured Destruction is a strategic standoff in which both sides could annihilate each other, so neither strikes first. It kept the Cold War from turning nuclear and has helped restrain India and Pakistan during crises. The same logic appears in business, where rivals like Apple and Samsung depend on each other.

Recognise when you and another party could seriously harm each other, in a partnership, contract, or negotiation. Shared vulnerability is a reason to seek cooperative solutions and keep competition within bounds, rather than taking actions that would damage you both.

stories.title: India and Pakistan at the brink

name: Polarity
one_liner: Once an issue grows two charged ends, everything gets pulled towards one or the other.
teaser:
In chemistry, polarity is how electrical charge is spread across a molecule, creating positive and negative ends. As a mental model, it describes how issues and groups split into opposing camps, like France during the Dreyfus Affair or Bud Light's customers in 2023.

Use it to anticipate when a decision might divide people. Break workplace debates into smaller questions, seek balanced financial advice, and look for shared values in family disagreements. Not every split is false, so take a stand thoughtfully rather than letting the pull decide.

name: Redline
one_liner: A limit decided in advance stops you giving ground one small step at a time.
teaser:
A Redline is a predetermined limit that signals serious consequences if crossed. It turns vague preferences into firm rules, guarding you against gradual drift and pressure in the moment.

Set redlines before negotiations, money decisions or difficult conversations, write them down, and state them clearly. Then enforce them calmly. Use them sparingly, because unenforced lines erode credibility and rigid lines can trap you when circumstances change.

name: Sayre’s Law
one_liner: The smaller the stakes, the more bitter the fight can become.
teaser:
Sayre's Law says the fiercest fights often happen over the smallest stakes. Astronomers still argue about whether Pluto is a planet, though nothing about Pluto changed, and two cartoon rabbit owners went to court before a real disaster put it in perspective.

Use it by asking what actually changes if either side wins. If the answer is almost nothing, use a quick decision rule and move on, and look for the respect or identity issue hiding beneath the argument.

name: Strawman Fallacy
one_liner: Beating a weaker version of someone’s argument proves nothing about the real one.
teaser:
The Strawman Fallacy distorts an opponent's argument into a weaker version that is easy to knock down. In 1860, Bishop Wilberforce argued against evolution, then mocked it with a jibe about ape grandparents.

Before you respond to someone, restate their view and check you have it right. Then answer the strongest version of their argument, not the cartoon. Your rebuttal will be fairer and far more convincing.

episode.title: Strawman Fallacy: When Arguments Are Made of Straw

name: Trojan Horse
one_liner: The most dangerous threats often arrive looking like gifts.
teaser:
A Trojan Horse is a deceptive strategy that disguises something harmful as harmless or welcome, so the target lets it through their own defences. It doesn't break the walls; it persuades defenders to open the gates.

Use it to spot hidden risks: ask what free offers give the giver, verify urgent payment requests through a number you know, and look inside before you trust. You can also flip it, wrapping good habits inside things you enjoy.

name: Zero-Sum vs Win-Win
one_liner: Many contests that look like fights over a fixed pie are chances to grow it.
teaser:
Zero-sum thinking treats every interaction as a fixed pie: more for you means less for me. Win-win thinking looks for ways to grow the pie so everyone gains. At Camp David in 1978, Egypt and Israel moved beyond a pure land-for-land standoff to a peace that served both nations.

When a situation feels like a contest, ask how the possibilities could be expanded. Look at what each side truly values, since different priorities often allow trades that leave everyone better off. Save zero-sum thinking for situations that are genuinely fixed, like a single prize.

name: Cooperation
one_liner: Together, with the right rules, we can do what none of us could do alone.
teaser:
Cooperation is individuals working together toward a shared goal for mutual benefit. In nature and in business, it lets small players achieve what none could manage alone, from Rochdale weavers pooling one pound each to carmakers sharing platforms.

To use it, look for partners whose strengths fill your gaps, agree on clear rules and shared rewards up front, and check in regularly so the deal stays fair. Cooperation runs on trust, so protect it.

name: Free Rider Problem
one_liner: If people can benefit without paying, many will let others pay.
teaser:
The free rider problem appears when people can benefit from something without contributing, from public radio to open-source software to a shared office kitchen. Each person assumes their small effort will not matter, so the shared good is underfunded or neglected.

To counter it, make contributions visible, keep groups small, assign clear owners, and reward those who pitch in. And when you rely on something free every day, consider paying your share.

name: Game Theory
one_liner: Your best move often depends on what others will do, and on what they expect you to do.
teaser:
Game theory models decisions as games with players, options and payoffs, where each person's outcome depends on the choices of others. It helps explain negotiations, pricing, auctions and cooperation, and why anticipating reactions often matters more than the best move in isolation.

To use it, put yourself in the other side's shoes before acting. Look for moves that make agreement their best option too, favor cooperation in repeated relationships, and set your limits in advance in competitive bidding.

name: Pirate Code
one_liner: Every group runs on rules of its own, and they predict behaviour better than the official ones.
teaser:
The Pirate Code is the set of rules, often unwritten, that governs how a group really works: how decisions are made, how rewards are shared and what gets you thrown out.

To use it, decode the real rules when you join any group, write down agreements about money and shared work early, and name hidden expectations before they turn into resentment.

name: Prisoner’s Dilemma
one_liner: Choices that are sensible for each person can add up to a worse result for everyone.
teaser:
The Prisoner's Dilemma shows how two people who would gain by cooperating are each tempted to betray the other, leaving both worse off. It began at RAND in 1950, where test players often cooperated anyway. European truck makers ran a price cartel until MAN confessed for immunity.

When trust is low, change the game: communicate, make clear agreements, reward cooperation, and remember that repeated interactions make trust far more valuable.

name: Social Norms vs Market Norms
one_liner: Putting a price on goodwill can make people care less, not more.
teaser:
Social norms run on goodwill and belonging. Market norms run on prices and contracts. Mixing them can backfire: adding money to a social exchange can make people care less, and the goodwill may not return.

To use it, think twice before paying for what people do out of pride, keep loans and gifts clearly separate, and choose the rulebook for each relationship on purpose.

name: Tit for Tat
one_liner: Start kind, answer in kind, forgive quickly, and others learn to cooperate with you.
teaser:
Tit for Tat means opening with cooperation, then copying what the other side did last. In Robert Axelrod's computer tournaments, this simple strategy beat cleverer rivals. But tariff wars, like the one that hit Harley-Davidson in 2018, show how mirroring can spiral into endless retaliation.

Start with goodwill, respond clearly to bad behaviour, and forgive quickly when the other side returns to cooperating. Add a little extra generosity to stop feuds from echoing on.

name: Tragedy of the Commons
one_liner: A resource everyone can use and no one looks after tends to be used up.
teaser:
The tragedy of the commons, popularized by Garrett Hardin in 1968, describes how individuals with open access to a shared resource can overuse it until it collapses, even when each choice seems rational. The North Atlantic cod fishery collapsed in 1992 after decades of overfishing, and shared attention at work can be drained by constant notifications.

Identify the commons around you, from shared spaces to team attention. Align incentives with care through clear rules, rotations, and recognition for those who maintain shared resources. Help others see the combined impact of small individual actions.

name: Trust
one_liner: Trust lets us cooperate without watching every move, but it lasts only when betrayal has a cost.
teaser:
Trust is our confidence in the reliability, honesty and competence of people and systems. It lets us delegate, cooperate and trade without checking everything ourselves, and it rests on track records, reputation and consequences for betrayal.

To use it, extend trust in small, testable steps, rely on systems with real accountability, and protect it in relationships by keeping even small promises.

name: Carrot and Stick
one_liner: Rewards and punishments change behaviour, but not always the way you planned.
teaser:
Carrot and stick is the use of rewards and punishments to motivate behaviour, named after the old way of driving a donkey. It is widely used, but its effectiveness depends on context. Heavy-handed incentives can boost short-term output while causing burnout, resistance or the loss of genuine motivation.

Before using rewards or penalties, ask whether the behaviour is better driven by intrinsic motivation, which crude incentives can undermine. When you use both, make sure they reinforce rather than contradict each other, start with positive reinforcement, and review whether the system is producing the results you want.

name: Distributive Justice vs Procedural Justice
one_liner: People can accept losing under fair rules, but resent even a good result reached unfairly.
teaser:
Distributive justice is about who gets what. Procedural justice is about how that was decided: clear rules, applied consistently, open to challenge. People often accept a disappointing result if they trust the process, and resent a good one reached in secret.

Use it whenever you hand out anything scarce, from bonuses to chores. Share your criteria before announcing results, agree on methods before splitting costs, and let a fair rule do the deciding. Fix the process first, then keep checking the outcomes.

name: Golem Effect
one_liner: Low expectations can drag people down to meet them.
teaser:
The Golem Effect describes how low expectations can drag performance down. When we expect little from someone, we tend to offer less challenge, attention and trust, and their results often fall to match our prediction.

To counter it, check whether everyone gets the same opportunities and feedback, avoid fixed labels with children and colleagues, and give people fresh chances to prove themselves. That includes yourself.

name: Managing to the Person
one_liner: People differ, so the best way to lead each of them differs too.
teaser:
Managing to the person means adapting your leadership to each individual's motivations, communication style, and strengths rather than using one approach for everyone. Lincoln handled each member of his team of rivals differently and held a fractious cabinet together through the Civil War.

Study the people you work with closely, as if writing a user manual for each relationship. Tailor feedback to how each person best receives it, whether direct, gentle, written, or spoken. Shape development paths and expectations around individual needs while keeping standards fair.

name: Peter Principle
one_liner: People tend to be promoted until they reach a job they cannot do well.
teaser:
The Peter Principle, from Laurence J. Peter's 1969 book, says people in hierarchies keep rising until they land in a role they can't perform well. Organizations reward success in the current job, not suitability for the next one.

Use it by judging candidates on the skills the new role needs, testing roles before you accept them and offering expert career paths outside management. People can grow into roles, so promote thoughtfully and support them well.

name: Principal-Agent Problem
one_liner: When someone acts for you, their interests and yours may quietly part ways.
teaser:
The principal-agent problem appears whenever you delegate: the agent may know more than you and want something different. Berle and Means showed in 1932 that managers, not owners, controlled many of the biggest US firms. At Olympus, executives hid about 1.7 billion dollars of losses from shareholders.

To use it, ask how anyone acting for you is paid, tie their reward to your outcome, and agree on simple check-ins. Aim for alignment and transparency, not suspicion.

name: Pygmalion Effect
one_liner: High expectations can lift people up to meet them.
teaser:
The Pygmalion Effect, or Rosenthal effect, is when higher expectations lead to better performance. When someone believes we'll succeed, they give us more attention, encouragement and challenge, and we often rise to meet it, as pupils did in Rosenthal and Jacobson's classroom study.

To use it, tell people what you believe they can achieve and back it with real responsibility. Speak about children with confidence, and surround yourself with people who expect the best of you. Low expectations work the same way, so watch yours.

name: Bystander Effect
one_liner: The more people who see a problem, the less likely any one of them is to act.
teaser:
The Bystander Effect is our tendency to hold back from helping when others are around. Each person assumes someone else will act, so responsibility spreads so thin that nobody takes it, in emergencies and in organisations alike.

To counter it, assume you are the one who must act. Assign clear owners in meetings, speak directly to one person in an emergency, and report problems even when many others can see them.

name: Chilling Effect
one_liner: Punish a few people visibly, and many more will silence themselves.
teaser:
The Chilling Effect is how a few visible punishments, or vague rules, make many people silence themselves. Its cost is hard to see, because nobody counts the ideas never shared or the risks never taken. The 1798 Sedition Act jailed only a handful of editors, yet made many more cautious.

Use it as a leader, parent or friend: thank the first person who raises bad news, notice which topics have gone quiet, and test your own fears with small, safe steps.

name: Dunbar’s Number
one_liner: We can keep up only about 150 real relationships at once.
teaser:
Dunbar's number, proposed by anthropologist Robin Dunbar, suggests humans can maintain around 150 stable relationships, with smaller inner circles of about 15 close friends and 5 intimate ones. Past that, ties thin into acquaintances.

Use it to guard time for the people who matter most, and to design teams and communities that stay human-sized. Treat 150 as a rough guide rather than a law, since people vary widely.

episode.title: Dunbar's Number: The Cognitive Limit of Human Connections

name: Groupthink
one_liner: A group that values harmony over honesty can talk itself into disaster.
teaser:
Group Think happens when a close-knit group values agreement over critical thinking. Members keep doubts to themselves, silence is mistaken for consensus, and confident teams talk themselves into serious mistakes.

To prevent it, collect opinions privately before discussion, assign someone to argue the other side, and invite outside voices. Make disagreement a normal part of the process rather than an act of disloyalty.

name: Hierarchical Organisation
one_liner: Layers of command let large groups act as one, at the cost of speed and candour.
teaser:
Hierarchical organization structures a group into layers, from small teams up to a single leader. The Roman legion built eight-man tent groups into centuries, cohorts and legions so orders moved fast. Its strength is clarity; its weakness is slow, distorted information and passive people at the bottom.

To use it, map who really decides in your workplace, break personal goals into layers, and choose deliberately how much structure a group needs. Too little breeds confusion. Too much breeds silence.

name: Power Vacuum
one_liner: When authority disappears, someone always rushes to fill the gap, often not who you would choose.
teaser:
A Power Vacuum occurs when authority collapses or goes unclaimed, leaving no clear structure for decisions. Rivals rush in, and the scramble can do more damage than the old order ever did.

Use it whenever you remove a leader, rule or routine. Name an interim owner before someone leaves, assign the tasks nobody owns, and replace habits instead of just dropping them. Fill gaps deliberately, or something else will fill them for you.

name: Activation Energy
one_liner: Good things often fail to happen not because they are hard, but because starting is.
teaser:
Activation energy is the minimum energy needed to start a chemical reaction. As a mental model, it explains why people delay worthwhile changes: the barrier is at the start, not the finish. The Erie Canal and Klarna both succeeded by lowering that first hump.

Use it to shrink first steps at work, automate savings, and prepare your exercise kit the night before. You can also raise barriers to habits you want to avoid. Be careful, though: some friction protects you from rash decisions.

name: Catalysts
one_liner: The right spark can make change happen faster, without doing the work itself.
teaser:
In chemistry, a catalyst speeds up a reaction without being consumed. As a mental model, it's any person, tool or event that accelerates change without doing all the work itself.

When progress stalls, look for the catalyst rather than more effort: a deadline, the right introduction, a workout partner. And be one for others. Just remember that catalysts only speed up what is already possible; they can't rescue a bad idea.

name: Compounding Effect
one_liner: Gains that build on earlier gains grow slowly, then dramatically.
teaser:
The Compounding Effect is the principle that gains build on previous gains, so growth accelerates over time. Luca Pacioli's rule of 72 captures it: divide 72 by your interest rate to estimate how many years it takes money to double.

To use it, start early and stay consistent. Invest automatically and reinvest returns, make small daily progress in learning, and nurture relationships with regular gestures. Remember that compounding works both ways, so watch out for debts and bad habits that snowball too.

name: Conditioning
one_liner: A signal paired often with something that matters comes to trigger the feeling alone.
teaser:
Conditioning is how we learn to link a cue with a response. Little Albert learned to fear a white rat paired with a loud noise, and Singapore Airlines linked a signature scent to the comfort of its cabins.

Use it to build habits by pairing something you enjoy with something you want to do more. Keep places and cues clean, like the bed for rest, and notice when apps and brands are training cravings into you.

name: Dopamine Loop
one_liner: The brain learns most from surprise rewards, and chases the cues that predict them.
teaser:
The dopamine loop is the brain's reward-learning system. Dopamine responds most strongly to unexpected rewards and to cues that predict them, as Wolfram Schultz's research showed, which is why it drives motivation and habit formation. Many apps and games are designed around these loops to keep us coming back.

Use the loop for good habits: make progress visible, break goals into small wins, and pair delayed-reward activities with something enjoyable now. Interrupt unhealthy loops by turning off notifications, setting tech-free times, and noticing when unpredictable rewards are pulling you back.

name: Forcing Function
one_liner: Shape the situation so the right action becomes the easiest, or the only, path.
teaser:
A forcing function is a commitment or constraint that makes the desired action unavoidable. Instead of relying on willpower, it reshapes the situation so follow-through becomes the only realistic path, through deadlines, public promises or designs that block mistakes.

To use it, build commitments into your environment: automatic savings, booked classes, shared deadlines. Choose constraints that push without crushing, and remember they reduce flexibility, so use them only for goals you are confident about.

name: Inertia
