one_liner: People and organisations keep moving along their current path until a real force makes them change.
teaser:
Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist changes in its motion. In life, habits, institutions and companies keep doing what they've always done long after the reasons have changed. Staying the course is often not a decision at all, just the absence of one.

To use it, regularly ask of each routine whether you would start it today. Make good choices the default, like automatic savings, so inertia works for you. And lower the barrier to starting new habits, because the first push is always the hardest. Stability has value, so change deliberately.

name: Momentum
one_liner: Progress builds on itself: early wins make the next ones easier, and slides gather speed too.
teaser:
In physics, momentum is mass times velocity: the heavier and faster something moves, the harder it is to stop. As a mental model, it describes how early wins attract confidence, support and resources that make the next win easier. The same force works in reverse, as setbacks and debts gather speed too.

To use it, sequence goals so a visible quick win comes first. Protect daily streaks in learning and habits, since restarting from a standstill is costly. Catch downward slides early, before they accelerate. And keep checking direction, because momentum can hide problems.

name: Bikeshedding
one_liner: Groups spend the most time on what everyone understands, and the least on what matters.
teaser:
Bikeshedding is the habit of debating small, easy-to-grasp details at length while complex, important decisions slip through. Parkinson's committee approved a reactor in minutes but argued for ages about a bike shed.

Match your attention to the stakes. Put time limits on low-stakes items, delegate small choices, and schedule the hard questions deliberately, even when they feel uncomfortable or unclear.

name: Law of Diminishing Returns
one_liner: Adding more of one thing eventually buys less each time, and can make things worse.
teaser:
The Law of Diminishing Returns says that adding more of one input, while everything else stays fixed, eventually yields smaller and smaller gains. Malthus saw it in farms; Subway saw it when new stores just took sales from old ones.

To use it, watch the margin: ask what the next hour, dollar or workout will really add. When gains shrink, move resources elsewhere or change the other inputs. More is only better until it isn't.

name: Leverage
one_liner: A small force in the right place can move a great weight, for better or worse.
teaser:
Leverage is the ability to achieve more with the same effort by applying it in the right place. A lever, a borrowed dollar, a reusable tool or a keystone habit can all multiply what you put in.

But leverage magnifies in both directions. Look for places where one action pays off many times over, and before borrowing or betting big, ask what happens if things move against you. Size your leverage to what you could survive losing.

name: Manager’s Schedule vs Maker’s Schedule
one_liner: One meeting costs a manager an hour, and a maker half a day.
teaser:
The Manager's Schedule vs. Maker's Schedule explains why interruptions cost creative people so much. Managers move between hourly meetings, but makers like writers and programmers need long uninterrupted blocks to do deep work.

Use it by clustering meetings into one part of the day, protecting long focus blocks on your calendar and asking before you interrupt someone deep in a task. The goal is not to ban meetings, but to place them where they cause the least harm.

name: Pareto Principle
one_liner: A small share of causes usually produces most of the results.
teaser:
The Pareto Principle, or eighty-twenty rule, says a few causes usually drive most of the effects: a few customers bring most revenue, a few defects cause most failures. The exact split varies, but the lopsidedness is common.

Use it to rank tasks, spending and time by impact, and tackle the vital few first. Just remember that finding the big causes is easier than fixing them, and the trivial many still count.

name: Top of Your Mind
one_liner: Whatever you think about in idle moments gets hours of free work.
teaser:
Top of Your Mind is the idea that most of us have one problem our thoughts return to when nothing else demands attention. Whatever sits there gets hours of free background thinking.

Choose that idea deliberately. Write down the problem you want to chew on, glance at it before a walk, and evict grudges or petty worries that try to steal the spot. Just don't let a healthy focus turn into an obsession.

name: Two-Front War
one_liner: Fighting two battles at once often means losing both.
teaser:
A Two-Front War is a struggle on two separate fronts at the same time. Resources and attention get split, and opponents on both sides simply need to hold while you wear thin.

Use it to sequence your battles. Finish one project before launching another, clear debt before a big new commitment, and avoid stacking major life changes in the same month. When two fronts are unavoidable, simplify one or find an ally.

name: Tyranny of Small Decisions
one_liner: Many small, sensible choices can add up to a result nobody wanted.
teaser:
The Tyranny of Small Decisions describes how individually reasonable choices, made one at a time, can combine into a result that few people would ever vote for, from eroded farmland to empty high streets.

To guard against it, judge repeated choices as policies rather than one-offs, look at the yearly total of small habits and commitments, and spend some of your money and time on the things you want to survive.

name: Velocity
one_liner: Progress is speed with direction; being busy is not the same as moving forward.
teaser:
Velocity is the rate at which something changes position, and unlike speed it includes direction. A car circling a track can be fast and still go nowhere. As a mental model, velocity reminds us that being busy is not the same as making progress toward the right goal.

To use it, review each week which tasks actually moved your most important goal forward. Point your extra money at one financial target at a time. And once a year, check whether your daily habits still point where you want your life to go. Aim first, then accelerate.

name: Hofstadter’s Law
one_liner: It always takes longer than you expect, even when you allow for that.
teaser:
Hofstadter's Law says it always takes longer than you expect, even when you take the law into account. We picture the smooth path and forget the surprises, interruptions and dependencies that pile up.

To use it, break tasks into small pieces, check how long similar work really took before, add a buffer, and share the later date. Treat your first estimate as a best case, not a forecast.

name: Minimum Viable Product
one_liner: Build the smallest thing that works, then learn before investing more.
teaser:
A Minimum Viable Product is the simplest version of an idea that still gives early users real value. Its purpose is learning: testing your riskiest assumption cheaply before you pour in serious time and money.

Use it everywhere. Try a career with a weekend of volunteering, test a side business with a dozen products, or start a habit at ten minutes a day. Then listen to what the real world tells you, and build from there.

name: Mythical Man-Month
one_liner: Adding people to a late project usually makes it later.
teaser:
The mythical man-month, from Fred Brooks, explains why adding people to a late project often slows it down: newcomers need ramp-up time, and every extra person adds coordination overhead. Some work simply cannot be split up, which is why small, focused teams often deliver more.

Before adding resources, ask whether the task can really be divided or must happen in sequence. Reduce coordination costs with clear documentation, independent components, and simpler communication. When a project slips, consider trimming scope or extending timelines instead of adding staff.

name: Perfect is the Enemy of Good
one_liner: Waiting for the ideal can cost you the useful.
teaser:
Perfect is the Enemy of Good means that waiting for the ideal solution can block a good one that would already create value. Endless polishing costs time, money and opportunities, and sometimes means the work never ships at all.

Use it by defining good enough before you start, choosing the workout you'll actually do and starting with a reasonable money plan. Just recognize the tasks, like safety-critical work, where near perfection truly matters.

name: Premature Optimisation
one_liner: Polishing before you understand wastes effort and locks in mistakes.
teaser:
Premature optimization is pouring effort into making something efficient before you understand where the real bottlenecks are, or whether it's needed at all. Donald Knuth warned programmers about it in 1974; Webvan built a billion dollars of warehouses before proving demand and went bankrupt.

To use it, ship a rough version first, start simple habits before perfecting plans, and focus on the few big levers. Measure, find the critical few parts, then optimize those.

name: Unforced Error
one_liner: Many of our worst setbacks are mistakes nobody forced us to make.
teaser:
An Unforced Error is a mistake that comes from our own carelessness, haste or poor communication, not from an opponent or bad luck. In many contests, the winner is simply the one who makes the fewest avoidable slips.

Use it by making instructions impossible to misread, pausing before speaking under stress, and automating away easy mistakes like late payments. When reviewing a failure, ask which parts were forced and which you handed yourself.

name: Algorithms
one_liner: Clear steps solve a problem the same way every time.
teaser:
An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem, like a recipe for a computer. The word comes from the 9th-century mathematician Al-Khwarizmi. Today algorithms quietly shape our lives, from GPS routes to Instagram feeds that optimise for engagement and decide what we see.

Remember that your feeds are curated, so think critically about what you are shown and be intentional with your habits and data. Borrow algorithmic thinking for your own problems too: break complex tasks into clear, repeatable steps, from your morning routine to your work processes.

name: Boots on the Ground
one_liner: To understand or change a place, you have to be there.
teaser:
Originally a military term for ground troops in a combat zone, Boots on the Ground now means being physically present to understand a situation. Rome's lasting hold on Britain came from staying, not raiding, and Howard Schultz turned Starbucks around by visiting stores and listening to staff.

Before big decisions, seek direct experience instead of relying only on second-hand reports. Shadow someone before a career change, use your own product, or visit the place where the problem actually happens. Show up in person, since presence reveals what spreadsheets miss.

name: Cargo Cult
one_liner: Copying the look of success rarely delivers the real thing.
teaser:
A Cargo Cult copies the form of success but misses the cause. Richard Feynman used the image of islanders building mock runways to warn about research that looks scientific but lacks honest self-criticism.

Before adopting a habit, process or tool because a winner uses it, ask what actually produces the result and whether that cause exists in your situation. Copy to learn, then keep asking why, and drop the parts that are only decoration.

name: Commandos
one_liner: Different stages of growth need different kinds of people.
teaser:
The Commandos model says organisations need different types of people at different stages. Commandos are scrappy pioneers who thrive in chaos and create something new; infantry systematise and scale it; police optimise and maintain it. Teams often struggle when they need one type but have another.

Know your natural role: do you love chaos, scaling, or stability? Match yourself to a project's phase, whether innovating, scaling, or optimising. And watch for transitions between phases, since that is when teams struggle most and when it may be time to hand over the baton.

name: Crowdsourcing
one_liner: Many people, each giving a little, can solve what a few experts cannot.
teaser:
Crowdsourcing taps the collective intelligence of many people, usually online. The term was coined by Jeff Howe in 2006, and examples range from Wikipedia's volunteer editors to Lego's fan-designed sets and the Netflix Prize, which offered a million dollars to improve its recommendations.

When facing a complex choice, ask your network or relevant communities for input to gain perspectives you might miss. Use crowd-built resources to learn new skills, and for community projects, invite a diverse group in early, since many minds often produce better ideas and execution.

name: Directly Responsible Individuals
one_liner: Every outcome needs one named owner, or it becomes nobody’s job.
teaser:
Directly Responsible Individuals are named owners for outcomes. When everything is everyone's job, nothing gets done. Admiral Hyman Rickover made individuals personally accountable across the US nuclear navy, and Haier split itself into micro-enterprises, each with an owner and its own results.

End meetings by naming one owner and a date for each task. Assign household bills and group plans the same way. Just remember ownership isn't blame: owners need support, resources and the authority to act.

name: Divide and Conquer
one_liner: Split a big opponent or problem into parts you can handle one at a time.
teaser:
Divide and Conquer tackles an overwhelming challenge by splitting it into smaller parts that can be handled independently and then recombined. Alexander the Great defeated Persian forces piece by piece, and Toyota improved manufacturing one component at a time before linking it all together.

Break big projects at natural seams: chapters, rooms, or distinct skills. Choose a smart order, considering dependencies and quick wins that build momentum. And keep the whole in view, checking regularly that progress on each piece still fits the overall goal.

name: Double-Entry Bookkeeping
one_liner: Every transaction has two sides, and recording both keeps the books honest.
teaser:
Double-entry bookkeeping records every transaction in at least two accounts, as a debit in one and a credit in another, so the books always balance. Popularised in Renaissance Italy, it creates a self-checking system that exposes errors and gives a complete picture of where value comes from and goes.

Apply double-entry thinking to everyday decisions: for every gain, ask what it costs, and for every expense, ask what you receive. Keep track of both sides of your time, money and commitments, and use mismatches as a cue to look closer at what might be missing.

name: Entropy
one_liner: Left alone, things drift towards disorder; order has to be paid for.
teaser:
Entropy is a measure of disorder in a system. The second law of thermodynamics says that in an isolated system it tends to increase. Order is never free: desks, budgets, friendships and companies all decay unless someone keeps spending energy to maintain them.

To use it, schedule maintenance before things break. Hold a weekly review at work, audit recurring charges every few months, and keep a steady rhythm of contact with the people you love. Not all mess is bad, so choose which kinds of order are worth paying for.

name: Institutional Knowledge
one_liner: Much of what an organisation knows lives in people, not documents.
teaser:
Institutional Knowledge is the practical understanding an organisation builds over time, its unwritten rules, lessons and skills. Most of it lives in people's heads, so it can disappear quietly when they leave or stop practising.

Protect it by interviewing departing colleagues, writing simple guides for systems only one person understands, and keeping skills alive through practice and teaching. Keep what still works and drop what doesn't.

name: Parallel Processing
one_liner: Split work into parts that can run at once, and finish sooner.
teaser:
Parallel processing breaks a big job into pieces worked on simultaneously. In the 1930s, hundreds of human computers split huge calculations into simple parallel steps; today, Cerebras packs hundreds of thousands of cores onto one chip.

To use it, run independent chores side by side, split team projects so people can work at once, and plan how the pieces will come back together. Keep deep thinking and real conversations single-tasked: attention doesn't divide well.

name: Replication
one_liner: Copying lets one success spread far, and it spreads the flaws just as faithfully.
teaser:
Replication is the process of copying or reproducing something, from DNA to books to business models. Gutenberg's identical printed pages let ideas spread consistently, and Aravind Eye Care copied an efficient surgery model across many hospitals.

Use it when you find something that works. Turn your best work into a template, copy proven money habits before tweaking them, and model the behaviour you want your family to repeat. But test before you multiply, because a faithful copy spreads hidden errors just as faithfully as strengths.

name: Comparative Advantage
one_liner: Do what costs you least to do, even if you are best at everything.
teaser:
Comparative advantage is the ability to produce something at a lower opportunity cost than others. David Ricardo showed in 1817 that England and Portugal both gained by specialising, even though Portugal was better at making both wine and cloth.

Use it to decide what to do yourself and what to hand off. Keep the tasks where your edge is largest, calculate what your hours are worth before doing everything yourself, and divide household chores sensibly. Just keep enough breadth to adapt, and make sure the gains are shared fairly.

name: Deliberate Practice
one_liner: Skill grows from focused work on weaknesses, not from hours alone.
teaser:
Deliberate Practice is a focused way to improve. Instead of simply logging hours, you target specific weaknesses, work at the edge of your ability, and use quick feedback to correct mistakes. Experience alone rarely creates expertise.

To apply it, pick one narrow skill, practise in short intense sessions, record or measure your attempts, and adjust after each round. Spend most of your time on what you're worst at, not what you enjoy.

name: Divergent Thinking vs Convergent Thinking
one_liner: Open up the options, then close them down.
teaser:
Divergent thinking means generating lots of possible ideas without judging them. Convergent thinking means evaluating those options and narrowing down to the best one. Trying to do both at once kills good ideas before they can grow.

Separate the phases on purpose. Brainstorm first with a no-criticism rule, then switch to choosing with clear criteria. It works in meetings, money decisions and family plans alike.

name: Generalist vs Specialists
one_liner: Breadth helps you adapt; depth helps you excel. The mix depends on your world.
teaser:
This model weighs breadth against depth. Generalists connect ideas across fields and adapt quickly to change. Specialists master the details and solve hard problems that demand precision. Each has strengths, and each has costs.

To use it, ask how fast your world is changing and how much depth your problem needs. Build a T-shaped skill set, bring in specialists for complex decisions, and mix both types on your teams.

name: Potential Energy
one_liner: Stillness is not emptiness: value can be stored, waiting to be released.
teaser:
Potential energy is energy stored in an object because of its position or configuration, like water held behind a dam or a drawn bow. As a mental model, it reminds us that stillness is not emptiness: unused skills, savings, relationships and dormant brands can all hold enormous stored value.

To use it, look for abilities and assets you've built but never put to work, and find the project that would release them. Build reserves like emergency savings and trust before you need them. Then direct the release carefully, because potential only matters once it becomes action.

name: Resonant Frequency
one_liner: Small pushes in the right rhythm can build into enormous effects.
teaser:
Every object has a natural frequency at which it vibrates most strongly. Push it in rhythm with that frequency and each push adds to the last, which is why marching soldiers once brought down a bridge. As a mental model, resonance shows that timing and rhythm can matter more than raw force.

To use it, time your requests to the natural cycles of your team, and learn with spaced repetition that matches how memory fades. In heated arguments, break step deliberately so reactions stop amplifying. Resonance is hard to predict, so test, observe and dampen early.

name: Spacing Effect
one_liner: We remember more when learning is spread out than when it is crammed.
teaser:
The Spacing Effect shows that we remember more when we revisit material in shorter sessions spread across days or weeks, instead of cramming it all at once. Each spaced review strengthens retention and understanding, which is why tools like Anki and Duolingo schedule repetitions over time.

Break learning into small, regular sessions and review key ideas at growing intervals. Use a calendar, reminders, or a spaced repetition app to stay consistent. The same rhythm works for skills, fitness, reading, and music: a little often beats a lot at once.

name: Specialisation
one_liner: Focusing on a narrow task makes each person far more productive.
teaser:
Specialization means concentrating on a narrow range of tasks to become more efficient and skilled. Adam Smith's pin factory showed how dividing work into steps multiplied output, and focused companies like Gong and Vanta build depth broad competitors struggle to match.

In your career, consider a T-shaped approach: deep expertise in one area plus working knowledge of related fields. On projects, divide work according to people's strengths. Stay alert to change, since over-specializing in a shifting field can leave you exposed, so keep enough flexibility to adapt.

name: Barriers to Entry
one_liner: The harder a market is to enter, the longer those already inside can keep their profits.
teaser:
Barriers to entry are the obstacles that make it difficult for new competitors to enter a market, such as high costs, regulation, patents, scale or network effects. They explain why some businesses stay protected for decades and why some markets are so hard to break into.

Before starting something new, map the barriers you will face, from financial to technical to social, and plan how to overcome each. In your own career or business, build barriers others would find hard to copy, such as rare skills, strong relationships and proprietary know-how.

name: Center of Gravity
one_liner: Find the one point everything depends on, then protect it or aim there.
teaser:
In physics, the center of gravity is where an object's weight is concentrated. As a mental model, it's the core source of strength in any system, the hub everything else depends on.

Use it to focus. Protect the activity that drives most of your results, guard the habit that holds the others up, like sleep, and look for the other side's real concern in a negotiation. Revisit it often, because centers can shift over time.

name: Economies of Scale
one_liner: When fixed costs are spread over more units, each one becomes cheaper to make.
teaser:
Economies of Scale are the cost advantages of producing more. Fixed costs, like a ship or a factory, are spread over more units, and bigger operations buy in bulk and specialize. Malcom McLean's container ship and Gustavus Swift's refrigerated beef both used scale to slash costs.

Use it in daily life: batch cook, reuse templates, share tools and car rides. But watch the limit, when size brings slow decisions and coordination becomes harder than doing it alone.

name: Moats
one_liner: Lasting success needs a structural defence, not just a moment of brilliance.
teaser:
A moat is a durable competitive advantage that keeps rivals at bay, a term popularized by Warren Buffett. Moats come from network effects, proprietary technology, brand loyalty, switching costs, or cost advantages, and the best ones deepen over time, as with ASML's lead in advanced chipmaking machines.

In your own work, build advantages that are hard to copy: rare expertise, systems clients rely on, and efficient processes that compound. When evaluating a business, ask what protects its profits and whether that protection is widening or shrinking.

name: Niches
one_liner: You don’t have to win everywhere; fit one need better than anyone else.
teaser:
A niche is the specific role an organism plays in its ecosystem: what it eats, where it lives and how it fits alongside others. Species that specialize avoid head-on competition and thrive.

Apply it by finding the space where your mix of skills is rare, focusing your spending and effort on what truly matters, and appreciating the different roles people play in your life. Keep watching for change, because niches can shift.

name: Punching Above Your Weight
one_liner: Resources set the odds, but a smaller side can win by choosing where to fight.
teaser:
Punching above your weight means getting results out of proportion to your resources. Underdogs usually win by choosing contests where their strengths count and a bigger rival's advantages shrink.

To use it, compete where speed, focus or local knowledge matter more than size. Concentrate limited resources on one goal, and let steady effort compound over time.

name: Secrets
one_liner: The most valuable insights are important truths that most people do not yet believe.
teaser:
As a mental model, popularised by Peter Thiel, a secret is not gossip but an important truth few people yet see. Great businesses and discoveries are often built on one, like Airbnb's insight that people would happily stay in strangers' homes, an idea that sounded absurd at first.

Question conventional wisdom and look for what others in your field overlook. Diverse perspectives help, since secrets often appear when familiar problems are viewed from new angles. And when you believe you have found one, have the courage to act on it before it becomes obvious.

name: Seizing the Middle
one_liner: Whoever controls the point that everything must pass through holds power beyond their size.
teaser:
Seizing the middle means occupying the central position that others must pass through, giving influence beyond your size. The Medici became central to European finance by connecting markets, and card networks like Mastercard sit between banks and merchants, earning from transactions without owning either side.

Look for junctions where value and information flow: bridge different groups in your network, build skills where specialties intersect, and take on coordinating roles at key points in your organization. A central position is powerful, so use it to create value for both sides.

name: Sustainable Competitive Advantage
one_liner: An edge only matters for long if rivals cannot copy it quickly.
teaser:
A sustainable competitive advantage is a strength rivals cannot easily copy, letting an organization outperform for years rather than months. The Venice Arsenal's shipbuilding system lasted for centuries, and platforms like Zapier built networks of integrations that are slow to replicate.

In your career, build skills that are valuable, rare, and hard to imitate, often by combining abilities into a unique stack. Choose systems and habits that improve with use and compound over time. Compete where your particular circumstances, network, and experience give you an edge.

name: Trademarks
one_liner: A distinctive sign becomes a promise that customers learn to trust at a glance.
teaser:
Trademarks are names, logos, and designs that identify who stands behind a product. Beyond legal protection, they are mental shortcuts that signal consistent quality, lowering the effort needed to choose. Coca-Cola's contour bottle became so recognizable that it was registered as a trademark in its own right.

Use trademark thinking to judge products: established brands have a reputation to protect, while lookalike names and inconsistent branding can be warning signs. In your own work, develop consistent, distinctive elements in style and approach so people recognize and trust what you make.

name: Adverse Selection
one_liner: When one side knows more about quality than the other, the best tend to leave and the worst stay.
teaser:
Adverse selection happens when one side of a deal knows more about quality or risk than the other. Buyers who cannot tell good from bad pay average prices, which drives away the best sellers. George Akerlof showed how this can unravel the used-car market.

Use it when hiring, buying insurance, lending or trading with strangers. Ask who knows more and who your terms will attract. Reduce information gaps with inspections, honest disclosures, trials and guarantees, just as CarMax did.

name: Apostle Model
one_liner: Satisfied customers drift away; only delighted ones bring others with them.
teaser:
The Apostle Model sorts customers by satisfaction and loyalty. Apostles are so delighted they keep buying and bring others with them, while unhappy terrorists warn people away. Research at Xerox found totally satisfied customers were six times more likely to buy again than merely satisfied ones.

Use it to decide where effort pays off: lift good experiences into great ones, look after the people already championing you, and listen hard to critics before their frustration spreads.

name: Churn
one_liner: Growth means little if customers leave as fast as they arrive.
teaser:
Churn measures how quickly customers cancel or stop buying. It compounds quietly: if people leave as fast as you win them, growth becomes expensive motion. Researchers Reichheld and Sasser found that small cuts in customer defections could raise profits sharply, because loyal customers cost less and buy more.

Apply it to your own life: cancel subscriptions you wouldn't buy again, call clients who drifted away, and keep old friendships warm before they go cold.

name: Customer Development
one_liner: Treat every idea about customers as a guess, and test it with real people early.
teaser:
Customer development is the practice of discovering what customers truly need by testing ideas with them early, instead of building first and hoping. David McConnell noticed buyers loved his free perfume more than his books and founded what became Avon.

Use it whenever you create something for others. Show rough versions to real users, validate side projects with small sales before investing, and listen for what people you love actually want. Customers cannot always imagine new things, so combine their feedback with your judgement.

name: Jobs to be Done
one_liner: People do not buy products; they hire them to make progress in their lives.
teaser:
Jobs to be Done says customers hire products to get a job done in a specific situation. Clayton Christensen's team found many morning milkshakes were hired to make a dull commute bearable, and Hilti realized builders wanted working tools, not drill ownership.

Use it at work, with money and in relationships: ask what situation someone is in, what progress they want, and what they'd fire to hire you. Then design for the job, not the product.

name: Lock-in
one_liner: Today’s convenient choice can become tomorrow’s trap when leaving costs too much.
teaser:
Lock-in happens when you become so dependent on a product, standard or supplier that leaving costs too much in money, time, data or compatibility, even when something better exists.

Before you commit to a tool, contract or platform, ask how you would get out. Review your subscriptions regularly, prefer open formats, and question whether you stay by choice or by inertia. And flip it around: make your good habits the ones that are hard to quit.

name: Loss Leader Strategy
one_liner: A price can be a doorway, not a destination: the bargain is meant to lead you somewhere.
teaser:
The Loss Leader Strategy prices one product at or below cost to draw people in, then earns its profit on everything else they buy. Supermarkets, game consoles and free trials all rely on it, but it only works if the follow-on sales really arrive.

As a shopper, follow every bargain to its destination and budget for the whole journey. As a seller or freelancer, choose an entry offer that opens a relationship, and plan how it grows into properly priced work.

name: Loyalists vs Mercenaries
one_liner: Discounts buy attention quickly, but they rarely buy commitment.
teaser:
Loyalists vs. Mercenaries sorts customers, supporters and team members by why they stick around. Loyalists stay because they value what you offer and recommend you to others. Mercenaries stay only while your price or perk beats the alternatives.

Discounts can buy attention but rarely commitment. Invest in what builds real attachment, such as quality, recognition and care, and know which group you are serving before you spend money trying to keep them.

name: Personas
one_liner: You design better for people when you picture a specific person rather than “users”.
teaser:
Personas are fictional but research-based characters that represent distinct groups of users, such as Mailchimp's solopreneur versus its mid-market marketing team. They turn an abstract 'user' into a person with goals and pain points, making trade-offs explicit and keeping decisions grounded in real needs.

When designing a product, writing, or planning a service, ask which persona it serves and what they need. Creating personas also builds empathy for others' perspectives. You can even sketch a persona of your ideal self to clarify goals and the steps to reach them.

name: Pivot
one_liner: Change direction on what you have learned, while keeping what you are good at.
teaser:
A pivot is a structured course correction: you keep your vision and what you have learned, but change a core part of the plan. Slack began as a game company and pivoted to the internal chat tool its team had built, and Western Union grew from telegraphs into money transfer.

When something isn't working, avoid both stubborn persistence and starting over from scratch. Ask what you have learned and which strengths carry over, then change one key element, such as the customer, the product, or the method, while keeping your underlying goal.

name: Product/Market Fit
one_liner: When something truly meets a pressing need, people pull it towards them.
teaser:
Product/market fit, a term popularized by Marc Andreessen, is the point where a product meets a strong market need so well that demand pulls it forward. Red Bull found it by adapting a Thai energy drink for Western nightlife and sports, and HubSpot by giving small businesses a simpler alternative to enterprise tools.

Before investing heavily in a project, look for real pull: people asking to join, organic word of mouth, and repeat use. Apply the same lens to your career by seeking places where your skills meet genuine demand, and keep adjusting as needs change.

name: Crossing the Chasm
one_liner: What enthusiasts love, the mainstream still needs to see proven, complete and recommended.
teaser:
Crossing the Chasm, Geoffrey Moore's idea, says the hardest step for anything new is the jump from early adopters, who love novelty, to the pragmatic majority, who want something proven and complete. Many products stall in that gap, as TiVo's beloved recorder did.

Use it when spreading any new idea: don't stop at the fans. Pick one practical group, solve their problem fully, and let trusted pragmatists convince the rest.

name: First Mover Advantage
one_liner: Arriving first can be worth a fortune, but only if you can defend the lead.
teaser:
First Mover Advantage is the edge gained by being first into a new market: early customers, scarce resources, standards set on your terms, and sometimes your name becoming the name of the whole category.

But being first is only the opening move, and followers learn from your mistakes for free. Before rushing in, ask whether your lead can be locked in through habits, networks or scarce assets, or whether you would simply be paying more to go first.

name: Flywheel
one_liner: Many small pushes in the same direction build momentum that one big heave never could.
teaser:
A flywheel is a system where each push adds momentum and the parts feed one another. Michelin's free guide got people driving, which wore out tires, which funded better guides. The early pushes feel slow; later ones feel effortless.

To use it, find two or three activities that reinforce each other, in your career, your health or your friendships, and push a little every week. Be patient through the slow start, and check now and then that your wheel is still turning in the right direction.

name: Long Tail
one_liner: When shelf space is unlimited, many small niches can add up to more than a few hits.
teaser:
The long tail describes how many niche products, each selling in small numbers, can add up to a large market once shelf space and distribution limits disappear. Digital music unlocked demand for songs physical stores never stocked, and platforms like Faire help small shops find independent brands.

As a consumer, look beyond the mainstream for options that fit your needs more precisely. As a creator, remember that a specialized offering can be viable when you can reach scattered audiences online. Look for opportunities to connect dispersed buyers and sellers who struggle to find each other.

name: Metcalfe’s Law
one_liner: The value of a network grows much faster than the number of people in it.
teaser:
Metcalfe's Law, named after Ethernet co-inventor Robert Metcalfe, says a network's value rises roughly with the square of its users. Each new member can connect with everyone already there, so value multiplies rather than adds.

Use it to choose platforms where your people already are, to invest in tightly connected communities and to become someone who introduces others. Just remember not all links are equal, and big networks can fill with noise.

name: Network Effects
one_liner: Some products become more valuable every time another person starts using them.
teaser:
Network effects happen when each new user makes a product more valuable for all the others, as with phones, payment systems, marketplaces and social platforms. They can create winner-takes-most markets, and the hardest step is starting the network from zero.

Use the idea to pick tools and skills with strong communities, to build personal connections that compound, and to notice when a network is locking you in before you commit your money or time.

name: Power Law
one_liner: In many areas, a few things account for most of the results.
teaser:
The Power Law describes lopsided worlds: a few words, cities, apps or projects dominate, while most stay small. George Zipf found the most common English word appears about twice as often as the second. Rovio made 51 modest games before Angry Birds outearned them all.

When outcomes follow a power law, averages mislead. Identify the few tasks that drive most of your results, keep making low-cost attempts so you're around for the rare big win, and check first whether your situation is truly lopsided or just ordinary.

name: S-Curves
one_liner: New ideas spread slowly, then suddenly, then slowly again as the market fills.
teaser:
S-Curves describe how new technologies and ideas spread. Adoption starts slowly with a few early users, accelerates rapidly as the idea proves itself, then levels off as most people already have it. American television went from under one percent of homes in 1948 to nearly ninety percent by 1960.

To use it, notice where your skills and investments sit on the curve. Learn the next thing before your current skills plateau, and don't quit during the slow start of learning something new.

name: Supply and Demand
one_liner: Prices rise when more people want something than there is to go round, and fall when there is plenty.
teaser:
Supply and demand explains how prices are set: when demand rises relative to supply, prices tend to rise; when supply rises relative to demand, they tend to fall. It explains surging delivery fees during the pandemic, cheap fruit at harvest, and expensive tickets for popular concerts.

Time purchases for when supply is high and demand is low, like winter coats in spring. In your career, build skills that are in high demand and short supply, and use that position when negotiating. When planning ahead, ask how demographic or technological trends may shift the balance.

name: Technology Adoption Lifecycle
one_liner: People take up new things at different speeds, and each group needs a different reason to join.
teaser:
The Technology Adoption Lifecycle divides adopters into five groups: Innovators, Early Adopters, Early Majority, Late Majority, and Laggards. Smartphones followed this wave, and companies like Tesla rode it by starting with premium products for early adopters before moving to the mass market.

Use it to time your own adoption: wait for the early majority if you value reliability over novelty. Notice where your industry and skills sit on the curve to stay relevant. And when introducing a new idea, tailor your pitch to whether your audience embraces or resists change.

name: Winner Takes Most Markets
one_liner: When being biggest makes you more attractive, a small early lead can become lasting dominance.
teaser:
Winner Takes Most Markets form when the biggest option becomes more attractive simply because it is the biggest, thanks to network effects, shared standards or scale. One leader captures most of the customers and profit, and rivals share what is left.

Use it to see when early momentum matters most. Aim to be the obvious choice in a specific niche, pick platforms likely to last, and question whether a giant's lead is truly permanent.

name: Creative Destruction
one_liner: New ways of doing things grow by tearing down the old ones.
teaser:
Creative Destruction, popularized by economist Joseph Schumpeter, is how innovation makes existing products, companies and jobs obsolete. Frederic Tudor built a global ice trade that refrigerators later wiped out, and Britannica stopped printing after 244 years once the web arrived.

Use it to stay humble about success: learn new skills before old ones are replaced, let outdated habits go, and remember the human cost for people on the losing side of change.

name: Cultural Evolution
one_liner: Ideas, habits and tools evolve like living things, only faster: the useful spread and the rest fade.
teaser:
Cultural Evolution applies Darwin's logic of variation, selection, and inheritance to ideas, technologies, and customs. Culture changes far faster than genes, which is how we moved from smoke signals to instant messaging, and why companies like Blockbuster fade when they fail to adapt.

Stay adaptable and willing to update your ideas as the world changes. Think critically, since some ideas spread because they are catchy, not because they are good. And view other cultures with empathy: each has evolved its own solutions to its own circumstances.

name: Disruptive Innovations
one_liner: Giants are often toppled by cheap, simple newcomers they once thought too small to matter.
teaser:
A disruptive innovation starts at the bottom of a market or creates a new one by being simpler, cheaper or more accessible. Incumbents dismiss it, but it improves and moves upmarket. Nucor's mini-mills began with rebar, and M-Pesa served Kenyans banks ignored.

Use it to spot threats and opportunities that look too small to matter. Learn basic new tools early, test low-cost alternatives to expensive habits, and start your own learning small. Watch the trajectory, not just the starting point.

name: Generals Fighting the Last War
one_liner: The lessons of the last battle can leave you perfectly prepared for a fight that never comes.
teaser:
Generals Fighting the Last War describes how past success or pain locks us into old strategies. We prepare for the challenge we already faced, even as the world shifts, and end up ready for a fight that never comes.

To avoid it, regularly ask whether the conditions behind your favourite playbook still hold. Prepare for several possible futures, seek fresh perspectives, and treat history as a guide rather than a script.

name: Natural Selection
one_liner: The environment decides what thrives, and when it changes, so do the winners.
teaser:
Natural selection is the process by which organisms with traits suited to their environment survive and reproduce more, passing those traits on. Fitness is always relative: Britain's peppered moths turned dark when soot blackened the trees, then pale again when the air was cleaned.

Ask what your environment is rewarding right now. Audit your skills yearly, test several money habits and keep the ones that survive, and design surroundings where good habits fit. Selection is blind and slow, but you can adapt before the pressure arrives.

name: Only the Paranoid Survive
one_liner: Success breeds complacency, so look hardest for threats when things are going well.
teaser:
Only the Paranoid Survive, the phrase popularized by Andy Grove, holds that success breeds complacency. The people and organizations that last keep watching for threats and shifts in the rules, especially when things are going well.

Use it by scheduling regular reviews of your career, finances and health while times are good. Ask what could make your current position obsolete. Just keep it productive: alert enough to spot danger, calm enough to act.

name: Paradigm Shift
one_liner: Sometimes a whole field’s basic assumptions are wrong, and progress means replacing the frame.
teaser:
A Paradigm Shift, a term popularized by Thomas Kuhn, is when a field's basic assumptions are overturned, like discovering ulcers are caused by bacteria rather than stress. Old frameworks resist change until the evidence becomes impossible to ignore.

Use it by tracking results that don't fit, revisiting old beliefs about health and work, and questioning the stories you tell about yourself. Stay open, but demand strong evidence before you change the whole frame.

name: Red Queen Effect
one_liner: When everyone else keeps improving, you must keep running to stay in place.
teaser:
The Red Queen Effect is the idea that organisms must keep evolving just to hold their position, because competitors, predators and parasites are evolving too. Biologist Leigh Van Valen named it after Lewis Carroll's Red Queen, who had to keep running to stay in the same place.

In competitive settings, yesterday's advantage becomes today's minimum. Treat learning as maintenance, review savings against inflation, and keep refreshing your relationships. But choose your races: sometimes the smartest move is finding a niche outside the arms race.

name: Survival of the Fittest
one_liner: Success goes not to the strongest, but to whoever best fits the conditions.
teaser:
Survival of the Fittest describes how organisms best suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce. Fittest means best matched to current conditions, not strongest, and when conditions change, the winners change too.

Use it by regularly checking whether your skills, finances and habits still fit your real circumstances, and adapting early. Remember that it describes nature, not how people ought to treat each other.

name: Arbitrage
one_liner: When the same thing sells for different prices in different places, someone profits from closing the gap.
teaser:
Arbitrage is taking advantage of a price difference for the same asset or product in different markets, buying where it is cheap and selling where it is dear. Beyond creating profit, arbitrage makes markets more efficient, because as more people exploit a gap, it closes.

Regularly compare prices and opportunities across platforms and markets, whether for goods, services or job offers. Look for gaps others have overlooked, like a skill valued more highly in another field. Act quickly but carefully, because arbitrage opportunities tend to disappear once others spot them.

name: Idea Maze
one_liner: Breakthroughs come from exploring many paths and learning from every dead end.
teaser:
The Idea Maze pictures the journey from a first idea to something that works as a maze of decisions, with many dead ends. Success comes less from a perfect first idea and more from exploring systematically and noticing the right passage.

To use it, map the key turning points before you commit, log what you try and what happens, and watch for unexpected user behaviour. Treat every wall as information.

name: Joy’s Law
one_liner: However strong your team, most of the smartest people work for someone else.
teaser:
Joy's Law, named after Sun Microsystems co-founder Bill Joy, says that however brilliant your team is, most of the world's talent sits outside it. Your organization, friends and advisors are only a tiny slice of what people know.

Use it by building doors for outside minds: share stuck problems widely, run open challenges, ask people from other fields, and look beyond a single source of advice. Just remember outsiders lack context, so pair their ideas with inside knowledge.

name: Local Optimum vs Global Optimum
one_liner: Being the best in your neighbourhood can stop you finding a much higher peak beyond it.
teaser:
Local Optimum versus Global Optimum is the difference between the best solution in a small area and the best solution overall. Once you reach a local peak, every small step looks worse, so you stop exploring, as Swiss watchmakers did while quartz watches took over.

To use it, regularly step back and ask whether you're climbing the right hill. Compare your options against completely different approaches, not just tweaks, and try something new when you hit a plateau. Balance improving with exploring.

name: Luck Surface Area
one_liner: You cannot control luck, but you can widen the area it can land on.
teaser:
Luck Surface Area is the idea that your chances of good fortune grow with how much you do and how many people know about it. Every project you share and every conversation you start gives chance a bigger target.

Use it by sharing your work publicly, saying yes to small invitations and running many cheap experiments. Prepare to notice opportunities when they appear. Just protect your time and energy, because not every attempt will pay off.

name: Simultaneous Invention
one_liner: When the conditions are right, several people often reach the same idea at once.
teaser:
Simultaneous Invention, or multiple discovery, is when separate people reach the same breakthrough independently: Newton and Leibniz with calculus, Darwin and Wallace with natural selection, Bell and Gray with the telephone. It suggests progress grows from shared knowledge and timing more than lone genius.

If someone else is working on your idea, don't be discouraged; it often means the time is right. Stay close to developments in your field, share and build on others' work, and focus on execution and perseverance, since good ideas rarely stay exclusive for long.

name: Arms Race
one_liner: When rivals keep matching each other’s build-up, both spend more and neither ends up safer.
teaser:
An arms race is a pattern of competitive escalation where each side builds up out of fear that its rival is doing the same. The Anglo-German naval race before WWI drained both nations without giving either a decisive edge, and similar races appear in business, schooling, and social media.

Watch for competitions where you keep escalating even though nobody gains, and ask whether the race is still worth running. In conflicts, remember the other side may be escalating out of fear, not malice, which opens the door to de-escalation and cooperation.

name: Asymmetric Warfare
one_liner: A weaker side wins by refusing to fight on the stronger side’s terms.
teaser:
Asymmetric Warfare describes conflicts where one side has far fewer resources and wins by refusing to fight on the stronger side's terms. The Afghan mujahideen used terrain and local support against the Soviet army, much as nimble fintech startups now chip away at large banks.

When you face a bigger rival or a daunting challenge, don't copy their strengths. Lean on your own advantages, such as speed, focus, or fresh perspective, look for unconventional approaches and unlikely allies, and change the rules of engagement where you can.

name: Beachhead Strategy
one_liner: Win one small, defensible position first, then use it to push further.
teaser:
The Beachhead Strategy, named after the D-Day landings, means concentrating resources on one small, winnable target before expanding. Qualcomm focused on efficient mobile chips that Intel ignored, dominated that niche, and was entrenched when smartphones took off.

Facing a big goal, pick one area you can fully win first. Master a single habit before overhauling your lifestyle, or one core skill before branching out. Concentrate your resources there, then use that secure foothold as the launching pad for your next move.

name: Counter-Insurgency
one_liner: Persistent resistance is fed by something, and cutting off that supply works better than force alone.
teaser:
Counter-Insurgency is the mix of military and civilian effort used to defeat rebels who depend on a population for food, recruits and legitimacy. Force alone rarely works; removing support and addressing grievances does.

Apply it to any recurring problem by asking what keeps feeding it. Fix the process behind repeat complaints, remove the cues behind bad habits, and resolve the grievance behind a conflict. Pair firmness with fairness.

name: Flypaper Theory
one_liner: Draw a threat to a place of your choosing, and it stays away from what matters most.
teaser:
The Flypaper Theory says a force or resource placed in one spot can attract opponents, engaging them there and away from more valuable targets. It works only if the lure is sticky and you are strong at that spot.

Use it to channel distractions into a set time, contain risk with a separate low-limit card, and catch problems early. But before setting a trap, ask whether you can hold that ground if they arrive in full force.

name: Guerrilla Warfare
one_liner: A small, nimble player can beat a giant by choosing where, when and how to fight.
teaser:
Guerrilla Warfare shows how smaller forces can beat larger ones by avoiding head-on fights and using speed, local knowledge, and surprise. The Viet Cong did it with tunnels and hit-and-run tactics, and Dollar Shave Club took on Gillette with a $4,500 viral launch video.

Identify your unique advantages, such as being more nimble, personal, or specialised, and lean on them. Choose battles where you can make the biggest impact with the least resistance. And don't feel bound by how things are usually done; unconventional moves are where small players win.

name: Nash Equilibrium
one_liner: A stable outcome is one where nobody gains by changing course alone, even if all would gain together.
teaser:
A Nash Equilibrium is a situation where no player can do better by changing strategy alone, given what others are doing. John Nash defined it in 1950, aged 21. UK supermarkets matching Aldi's prices show it: cutting deeper invites matching, raising prices loses shoppers.

When a situation feels stuck, map each person's best response. Stable does not mean good, so look for ways to change the rules or coordinate with others to reach a better outcome.

name: Strategy vs Tactics
one_liner: Brilliant moves cannot rescue a weak plan, and a good plan fails without good moves.
teaser:
Strategy vs. Tactics separates the big picture from the immediate action. Strategy decides which goals matter and how you will win over time. Tactics are the specific steps and manoeuvres you take along the way. Brilliant tactics cannot rescue a poor strategy.

Use it whenever you feel busy but not effective. Check each task, workout or argument against your larger goal. Drop clever moves that lead nowhere, and make sure every small action points in the same direction as the plan.

name: War of Attrition
one_liner: Some contests are won not by the best blow, but by whoever can last the longest.
teaser:
A War of Attrition is a prolonged conflict where each side tries to wear the other down through sustained losses. The winner is usually whoever has deeper reserves, more patience or lower costs.

Before entering a long fight, count your reserves and your opponent's. Use attrition on your side to wear down bad habits with small, steady wins. And in feuds or disputes, ask whether victory is worth the cost, or whether settling early is wiser.

name: Base Rate Fallacy
one_liner: A vivid detail means little until you know how common the outcome is in general.
teaser:
The base rate fallacy happens when a striking detail makes us forget the background odds. Without knowing how common an outcome is overall, even accurate evidence, like a positive test or a strong pitch, can lead to the wrong conclusion.

Before judging, ask the base rate question: how often does this happen in general? Start from those odds, then adjust for the specifics. Move away from them only when the evidence is genuinely strong.

name: Bayes’ Theorem
one_liner: Change your mind in proportion to the evidence: a lot for strong clues, a little for weak ones.
teaser:
Bayes' Theorem describes how to update beliefs when new evidence arrives. You begin with a prior, then shift it according to how strongly the evidence points one way, so strong evidence moves you a lot and weak evidence only a little.

To use it, write down your starting estimate, ask how common something is before reacting to one result, and change your mind gradually as patterns emerge.

name: Central Limit Theorem
one_liner: Average enough random pieces and the averages settle into a predictable bell shape.
teaser:
The Central Limit Theorem says that if you take many random samples and average each one, the averages form a bell curve as samples grow, whatever the shape of the original data. That's why averages from good samples can estimate large populations.

To use it, judge people and investments over many results, not one, track health trends with averages, and distrust conclusions built on tiny samples.

name: Conditional Probability
one_liner: Odds are never fixed: they change the moment you learn something new.
teaser:
Conditional probability is the likelihood of an event given that another event has already occurred. New information changes the odds, sometimes dramatically, as the famous Monty Hall puzzle shows.

To use it, ask what a statistic means for someone in your situation, update your plans when conditions change, and consider people's circumstances before judging their behaviour.

name: Confidence Interval
one_liner: The honest answer to many questions is a range, not a single number.
teaser:
A confidence interval is a range around an estimate that is likely to contain the true value. Its width shows how uncertain the estimate is, and a ninety-five percent method captures the truth in about nineteen of twenty samples.

To use it, budget and plan with ranges, give colleagues honest estimates with bounds, and read health or poll results with their margins in mind.

name: Distributions
one_liner: A single number hides the shape of the spread, and the shape often matters more.
teaser:
A distribution describes the full spread of possible outcomes: where values cluster, how wide they range, and how often extremes appear. Two situations with the same average can have very different shapes, and the shape is often what matters for decisions.

To use it, ask about the range, not just the typical case. Plan your time, money and designs around the realistic spread, including the bad days. Gather several observations before judging, and remember that past patterns may not cover every future surprise.

name: Error Bars
one_liner: Every number comes with a margin of doubt, whether or not anyone draws it.
teaser:
Error bars mark the range around a measurement where the true value plausibly lies. Every number carries some uncertainty from small samples, imperfect tools or natural variation, and a precise-looking figure can hide a lot of wobble. Overlapping ranges mean a difference may not be real.

To use it, ask how sure a number is before acting on it. Give and request estimates as ranges, watch trends instead of single readings, and be wary of small samples. Remember that error bars cannot fix a biased method.

name: Frequentists vs Bayesians
one_liner: Probability can mean how often something happens, or how strongly you believe it will.
teaser:
Frequentists define probability as long-run frequency across repeated trials. Bayesians define it as a degree of belief that starts with a prior and updates as evidence arrives. Both are useful, in different situations.

Use frequency thinking when you can gather lots of repeat data, like commute times. Use Bayesian thinking for one-off, high-stakes choices: state your starting belief, then let every result, including every failure, move it.

name: Mean, Median and Mode
one_liner: “Typical” can mean three different numbers, and each one tells a different story.
teaser:
The mean is the ordinary average, the median is the middle value, and the mode is the most common one. They can differ dramatically. A few extreme values pull the mean, while the median stays steady, and the mode reveals what appears most often.

To use it, always ask which average you are hearing, especially for incomes, prices and returns. Use the median for typical experiences, the mode for popular preferences, and remember that no single summary shows the full spread of the data.

name: Normal Distribution
one_liner: Most things cluster around the middle, but the bell curve makes extremes look rarer than they are.
teaser:
The normal distribution is the classic bell curve: values bunch around the average and thin out symmetrically toward the extremes. Many natural measurements roughly follow it, which makes it a useful way to judge how typical or unusual a result is.

To use it, put single results in context before worrying or celebrating. But be careful with money and complex systems like markets, where extreme events happen far more often than a bell curve predicts. Prepare for the tails, not just the middle.

name: Probability Distribution
one_liner: Good decisions weigh everything that could happen, not just the single most likely outcome.
teaser:
A Probability Distribution maps the full range of outcomes, not just the most likely one. Ladislaus Bortkiewicz showed that deaths from horse kicks in the Prussian cavalry followed a steady, predictable pattern, and prediction markets like Polymarket turn prices into live probabilities.

Use it by estimating ranges instead of single numbers, planning budgets for rough months rather than average ones, and checking real base rates before reacting to vivid stories. Redraw your picture whenever new evidence arrives.

name: Regression to the Mean
one_liner: Extreme results tend to be followed by ordinary ones, because luck rarely repeats itself.
teaser:
Regression to the Mean explains why unusually good or bad results tend to be followed by more ordinary ones. In 1933 Horace Secrist wrote a book claiming business was sliding into mediocrity, but it was just this effect. DocuSign's pandemic surge also faded as normal life returned.

Before praising, blaming, investing or changing course after an extreme result, ask what would have happened anyway. Look at long track records, not single standout moments, and wait for enough data to spot a real shift.

name: Standard Deviation
one_liner: An average tells you the centre; the spread tells you how much to trust it.
teaser:
Standard Deviation tells you how tightly data cluster around the average. Karl Pearson coined the term in 1893, and Six Sigma, adopted by Larry Bossidy at AlliedSignal in 1994, used it to cut variation and defects.

Two things can share an average yet differ wildly in reliability. Look at the spread when planning commutes, comparing investments or building habits, and leave buffers for it. Just remember it can understate risk in lopsided, rare-event situations.

name: Variance
one_liner: Every process wobbles; the skill is telling ordinary wobble from a real warning sign.
teaser:
Variance measures how much results swing around their average. In 1924 Walter Shewhart drew the first control chart to separate everyday common-cause wobble from real, assignable problems. JR Central keeps average Shinkansen delays under a minute by attacking variation everywhere.

Learn the natural range of your numbers before reacting, smooth irregular spending into steady monthly amounts, and keep routines consistent so real problems stand out. Just leave room for the healthy variation that creativity needs.

name: False Negative
one_liner: A clean result should lower your concern, not end it.
teaser:
A false negative, or Type Two error, happens when a test or judgment wrongly reports that nothing is wrong. Because a negative result feels like closure, we stop looking while the real problem keeps growing out of sight.

To use it, treat a clean result as lowering your concern, not ending it. Combine different checks, take conflicting signs seriously, and follow up when symptoms or doubts persist, especially where missing something would be costly.

name: False Positive
one_liner: An alarm is a question, not an answer.
teaser:
A false positive, or Type One error, happens when a test or judgment flags something that is not actually present. Because we act on alarms, false positives lead to needless panic, treatment or accusation, and at large scale even small error rates create many wrong alarms.

To use it, treat an alarm as a question, not an answer. Seek independent confirmation before acting, especially when people could be harmed, and tune your alerts so the important ones still get noticed.

name: Falsification
one_liner: Trying to prove yourself wrong is the surest route to finding out what is right.
teaser:
Falsification means looking for the evidence that could show you're wrong. Michelson and Morley's failed hunt for the ether helped overturn a whole theory, and Harrah's casino tested every offer against a control group.

Use it by deciding in advance what result would prove your plan wrong, running small fair tests on your habits, and seeking the strongest case against your own story. Trust ideas more once they survive a real attempt to break them.

name: Hypothesis
one_liner: A good guess is one that reality can prove wrong.
teaser:
A hypothesis is a proposed explanation that makes a prediction reality can confirm or refute. It sits between a hunch and a fact, and its power comes from being falsifiable.

To use it, turn opinions into tests. State what you expect, decide in advance what result would change your mind, and try it on a small scale first, whether that's a sleep habit, a work process, or a business offer.

name: Inductive Reasoning
one_liner: Experience suggests what will happen next, but it can never promise it.
teaser:
Inductive reasoning is how we learn from experience: we see a pattern repeat and expect it to continue. It is essential, but its conclusions are only probable. A long streak of past observations cannot promise the future.

Use it wisely by asking how many cases you have, how varied they are, and what could break the pattern. Hold beliefs with confidence that matches your evidence, and keep a cushion for the day the trend reverses.

name: Meta-Analysis
one_liner: Many small, uncertain studies, pooled together, can give one clear answer.
teaser:
A meta-analysis pools the results of many separate studies on the same question into one overall estimate. Small studies are noisy and often inconclusive alone, but combined they can reveal clear benefits or hidden risks years earlier than any single trial.

To use it, look past single headlines and seek reviews of the full body of evidence. Combine your own small experiments and gather many independent sources before big decisions. But remember the result is only as good as the studies that go into it.

name: Null Hypothesis
one_liner: Assume a claim does nothing until the evidence forces you to think otherwise.
teaser:
The null hypothesis is the default assumption that a treatment, strategy or claim makes no difference. Instead of asking critics to disprove an idea, it makes the idea earn belief by producing results too surprising to be chance.

To use it, start skeptical of health products, workplace changes and investment claims. Compare against a fair baseline, and look for blinded or controlled tests. But remember that failing to find an effect is not proof there is none, since small tests can miss real effects.

name: Occam’s Razor
one_liner: When explanations compete, start with the simplest one that fits the facts.
teaser:
Occam's Razor, named after the 14th-century philosopher William of Ockham, advises that among competing explanations we should prefer the one that makes the fewest assumptions. It does not guarantee the simplest answer is right, but it trims away needless complexity and points us to the most likely starting point.

When something puzzles you, list your assumptions and see which you can remove. Check simple explanations first, such as workload or unclear instructions when a colleague seems disengaged, before reaching for complicated theories. Add complexity only when the evidence demands it.

name: P-Values
one_liner: A small p-value says a result would be surprising by chance, not that an idea is true.
teaser:
A p-value measures how surprising your results would be if nothing real were going on. A small p-value counts as evidence against the no-effect assumption, but it does not tell you the probability an idea is true or how big an effect is.

To use it, ask how often chance alone could produce what you see. Look at the size of the effect, the sample behind it and whether others have replicated it. Be especially wary of impressive results in small or accidental slices of data.

name: Placebo Effect
one_liner: Belief and care can make people feel better, even when the treatment itself does nothing.
teaser:
The Placebo Effect shows that expectation and care can change how we feel, especially with pain and fatigue. Henry Beecher reported that about a third of patients improved on placebo, though later critics showed much of that was natural recovery.

Use it by building calming rituals alongside real treatment, and by judging remedies, products and new strategies against a fair comparison. A good feeling is welcome, but it isn't proof that something works.

name: Randomised Controlled Experiments
one_liner: Let chance decide who gets the treatment, and any difference left is the treatment’s doing.
teaser:
Randomized Controlled Experiments split participants by chance into treatment and control groups, so hidden differences cancel out. The 1954 Salk polio trial involved about 1.8 million children, and Ctrip randomized staff by birthday to test working from home.

Use the idea in daily life by flipping a coin to decide when to try a new habit, tracking the results, and comparing honestly. Randomization stops you fooling yourself, though some questions can't be ethically randomized and small tests can be noisy.

name: Scientific Method
one_liner: Let evidence, not authority or wishful thinking, decide what you believe.
teaser:
The scientific method is a loop: observe, form a hypothesis, design a test that could prove you wrong, analyse the results, and refine. Its strength is that it lets evidence overrule authority and wishful thinking.

Apply it to everyday choices by changing one variable at a time, tracking the results honestly, and being willing to drop ideas that fail. Most experiments won't work, and that's how you learn.

name: Statistical Significance
one_liner: A significant result is one that chance alone would rarely produce; it need not be big.
teaser:
Statistical Significance asks whether a result would be unlikely if there were no real effect. William Gosset, a Guinness brewer writing as Student in 1908, invented the t-test for small samples. In 2020, remdesivir significantly sped recovery, but its effect on deaths wasn't significant.

Before declaring a winner, ask whether you have enough data, how big the effect is, and whether it replicates. Significant doesn't mean important, and not significant doesn't prove there's no effect.

name: Systematic Review
one_liner: To know what the evidence says, gather all of it by rules set in advance.
teaser:
A Systematic Review gathers every relevant study on a question, judges each against the same rules, and combines the results. It protects us from cherry-picking the research we like or the headline we happened to remember.

Use it before big health, money or work decisions. Set your criteria first, collect evidence from many independent sources, include the dull results along with the dramatic ones, and let the overall pattern guide you. Remember that a review is only as good as the evidence it can find.

name: Causal Fallacy
one_liner: Two things happening together is not proof that one caused the other.
teaser:
The causal fallacy mistakes correlation or sequence for causation. Two events can appear together by chance, because a hidden third factor drives both, or because cause runs the other way. Crediting the wrong cause leads us to repeat what doesn't work.

When someone claims X causes Y, ask three questions: what else could explain it, which way does the cause run, and is there a fair comparison group?

name: Clustering Illusion
one_liner: Randomness is lumpier than we expect, so we see patterns where there are none.
teaser:
The clustering illusion is our tendency to see meaningful patterns in random data. True randomness produces streaks and clumps, and our brains rush to explain them, mistaking luck for skill or chance for cause.

To use it, ask whether chance alone could explain a streak, count the failures as well as the winners, and test a pattern with more data before betting on it.

name: Confounding Factor
one_liner: When two things move together, a hidden third factor may be pulling both strings.
teaser:
A confounding factor is a hidden variable that influences both the supposed cause and the supposed effect, making them look connected when they may not be. Summer drove both polio cases and ice cream sales.

To use it, ask what else changed when a result appears, check whether the people being compared started out alike, and trust randomised comparisons over simple before-and-after stories.

name: Correlation and Causation
one_liner: Patterns are where good questions begin, not where they end.
teaser:
Correlation and causation are not the same. Two things can move together because of coincidence, a hidden third factor or cause running the other way. Proving cause takes stronger evidence, like strength, consistency and dose-response.

To use it, question headlines that link habits to outcomes, test new ideas with fair trials before scaling, and ask marketers for real evidence of effect.

name: Regression Fallacy
one_liner: Inventing a cause for a return to normal is one of the commonest mistakes we make.
teaser:
The Regression Fallacy is the error of assuming an unusually high or low result will continue, or of crediting some action when results drift back toward average. Extreme outcomes usually contain a large dose of luck, and luck rarely repeats on cue.

Before rewarding, punishing or changing course after a dramatic swing, look at a longer track record. Ask whether you are seeing a new level or just a temporary peak or trough. Judge people, investments and remedies by patterns, not single moments.

name: Texas Sharpshooter Fallacy
one_liner: Draw the target after the shots and every shooter looks like a marksman.
teaser:
The Texas Sharpshooter Fallacy is painting the target after firing the shots: picking out clusters in data and ignoring everything else. The Bible Code found predictions in the Torah, but critics found similar ones in Moby-Dick.

Decide what you are testing before you look at the results. Ask what data was left out, and treat patterns found in hindsight as ideas to test, not conclusions already proven.

episode.title: Texas Sharpshooter Fallacy: When Randomness Masquerades as Skill

name: Anecdotal Evidence
one_liner: A vivid story shows that something happened once, never how often it works.
teaser:
Anecdotal evidence is proof drawn from individual stories and testimonials. Stories are vivid and persuasive, but they can't tell us how many people a remedy or tip failed, or what would have happened anyway.

When a story pushes you toward a decision, ask about everyone who isn't in it, and look for controlled studies or real data. Use stories to raise good questions, then let the evidence answer them.

name: Data Dredging
one_liner: Search enough data and some pattern will always turn up, by chance alone.
teaser:
Data dredging means trawling through a large dataset, testing comparison after comparison, until something lines up. With enough tries, coincidences are guaranteed, and they look just as convincing as real effects. That is how a football result once seemed to predict the stock market.

To avoid it, decide your question and your measure before you look. Count how many comparisons were made. Treat surprising patterns as leads, not conclusions, and confirm them on fresh data before you act on them.

name: Hasty Generalisation
one_liner: A few examples, however vivid, are not enough to support a sweeping rule.
teaser:
A Hasty Generalization turns a handful of cases into a broad rule. Phrenology grew from a few hand-picked skull observations, and Target assumed its US success would carry over when it opened 133 Canadian stores at once.

Before acting on a pattern, ask how many cases you really have and whether they are representative. Test small before scaling up, and hold early conclusions loosely until more evidence arrives.

name: Non-Response Bias
one_liner: The people who stay silent can change the answer as much as those who reply.
teaser:
Non-Response Bias happens when the people who answer a survey, review or feedback form differ in important ways from those who stay silent. Even a well-chosen sample can produce misleading results if only certain kinds of people reply.

Whenever you rely on responses, ask who did not answer and why. Treat low response rates as a warning sign, follow up with quieter people directly, and look for patterns across many reviews rather than the loudest stories. Silence is data too.

name: Overgeneralising from Small Samples
one_liner: Small samples swing wildly by chance, so their patterns often vanish when you look again.
teaser:
Overgeneralizing from Small Samples means drawing big conclusions from too little evidence. Small samples swing wildly by chance, so a handful of anecdotes or one tiny study, like the 36-student Mozart effect experiment, can create beliefs that later collapse.
